questions.subtopic: 3C Evidence collection. AI-listed requirements
questions.question: An IS auditor asked a generative AI tool to list the data-protection rules that apply to a client's patient-triage chatbot; it returned 14 requirements, each citing an article number. What should the auditor do FIRST?

options.A: Adopt the 14 requirements and their article numbers as audit criteria
options.B: Ask the tool to remove any requirement it is unsure about
options.C: Ask the tool to give a source link for each requirement
options.D: Check each requirement and article against the official legal text

questions.key_concept: Generative AI can confabulate citations; requirements it lists must be verified against official texts before they become audit criteria.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the tool's citations rest on and where the auditor can confirm them.
questions.correct_explanation: Generative tools can invent rules and article numbers that look exact, so the list is a lead, not criteria. Checking each item against the official text confirms that it exists and says what the tool claims before it shapes the audit. Asking for source links seems to add traceability, but the links are generated too and may be wrong; they still have to be opened and checked.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because article numbers look authoritative. But a tool can invent precise-looking citations, and unverified criteria could misdirect the whole audit.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it seems to filter out weak items. But a model's sense of its own certainty is unreliable; confident errors would stay in the list.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because links seem to make each item traceable. But generated links can be wrong or invented, and they still need to be opened and checked.

tips: Eliminate: A treats confident citations as proof, and B relies on the tool judging its own certainty.
Final two: D beats C because only the official text confirms a rule; generated links are more output that still needs checking.
Exam cue: generative AI can invent citations. Verify any law, standard or clause it names against the source before using it.

questions.subtopic: 3C Evidence collection. Checking extracted data
questions.question: An approved AI tool extracted weights from 8,000 scanned Ghanaian cocoa delivery notes and scored its confidence in each; the IS auditor plans to check only extractions below 90%. What is the GREATEST concern?

options.A: Extractions scored 90% or above can be wrong and go unchecked
options.B: Extractions below 90% may be mostly right, wasting checking effort
options.C: Handwritten notes may get lower confidence scores than printed ones
options.D: The 90% cutoff came from the auditor rather than the tool's vendor

questions.key_concept: AI confidence scores are self-estimates; using them to skip verification leaves confident errors untested in audit evidence.
questions.pre_read: Ask which errors the checking plan could never find.
questions.correct_explanation: A model's confidence score is its own estimate, and models can be confidently wrong, for example on unfamiliar layouts. Checking only low scores leaves high-confidence errors untested, and they flow straight into the audit evidence. Low-scored items that prove correct only cost time. The auditor should also test a sample of high-confidence extractions to measure their error rate.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because wasted effort is a real cost. But extra checks only cost time; unchecked high-confidence errors enter the evidence unseen.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because handwriting is harder to read. But lower scores send those notes to checking; the risk lies in errors scored high.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because vendors know their tools. But a vendor default is no more validated for these notes than the auditor's choice.

tips: Eliminate: D assumes a vendor default would be validated, and C describes items that the plan already sends for checking.
Final two: A beats B because extra checks only waste time, while confident errors pass into the evidence untested.
Exam cue: an AI confidence score is the model's self-estimate, not proof. Test a sample of high-confidence output too.

questions.subtopic: 3D Data quality and analytics. AI-assisted access review
questions.question: An IS auditor gave an approved AI assistant a Cypriot shipping line's leavers list and 60,000-line access export, several times its context window; it named 12 active leaver accounts. What should the auditor verify FIRST?

options.A: That the vendor's terms bar it from training on the export
options.B: That the prompt and the assistant's version are saved in work papers
options.C: That the assistant's result covers all 60,000 exported lines
options.D: That each of the 12 named accounts stayed active after departure

questions.key_concept: An AI assistant given more than its context window can silently process only part; the auditor confirms completeness before relying on the result.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether the answer covers every record or only the records the tool read.
questions.correct_explanation: A context window is the amount of input an assistant can process at once. Given more, assistants can silently read only part, then answer as if they saw everything. Reconciling the lines it processed to the 60,000 shows whether the 12 come from the whole population; if not, the test is rerun in batches that fit. Confirming the 12 is needed too, but it cannot reveal leavers in lines never read.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because audit data must stay confidential. But the assistant is approved, so its data terms were already assessed.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because documentation supports review. But saving the prompt records what was asked; it does not show whether every line was read.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because each named account must be confirmed before reporting. But that tests the hits; leavers in unread lines would stay invisible.

tips: Eliminate: B documents the work without testing it, and A reopens data terms the approval already covered.
Final two: C beats D because confirming the 12 tests only what was found; if lines went unread, the result cannot support a conclusion on the whole population.
Exam cue: before trusting an AI tool's answer about a population, reconcile what it actually processed to the source record count. Its own claim of full coverage is not evidence.

questions.subtopic: 3D Data quality and analytics. Regional pricing test
questions.question: Testing whether a Romanian lender priced borrowers fairly across regions, an IS auditor finds 6% of loans missing from the pricing model's log: timeouts priced by a fixed rule. What should the auditor do FIRST?

options.A: Proceed with the logged loans and record the 6% gap as immaterial
options.B: Add the rule-priced loans from the loan system to the population
options.C: Have the model owner rerun the timed-out requests through the model now
options.D: Limit the population to loans that the model itself priced

questions.key_concept: An AI decision population includes fallback decisions made when the model fails; define the population by the audit objective.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether the objective is about the model's outputs or the outcomes people received.
questions.correct_explanation: The objective is whether borrowers were priced fairly, and the fallback rule priced 6% of them, so those loans belong in the population. Timeouts may not fall evenly across regions, so leaving them out could hide the very pattern under test. Excluding them would suit a test of the model alone, but this objective covers every borrower's rate, including those the fallback set.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the gap looks small. But a gap with a known cause may be concentrated in some regions, so it cannot be assumed immaterial.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it fills the gap with model prices. But rerun prices are not the rates borrowers got, and today's model may differ.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the model did not set those rates. But the objective is how borrowers were priced, and the fallback rule priced those borrowers.

tips: Eliminate: C creates prices borrowers never received, and A accepts a known population gap without testing whether it matters.
Final two: B beats D because the objective is how borrowers were priced, and the fixed rule priced those borrowers; dropping them could hide a regional pattern.
Exam cue: an AI system's population includes its fallback path. Define it by the objective, not by which component decided.

questions.subtopic: 3D Data quality and analytics. Minutes-review tool
questions.question: An Omani group's audit team checked an AI tool that finds related-party dealings in English board minutes and now wants to use it on Arabic minutes. What should the chief audit executive require FIRST?

options.A: Rerunning the English test cases to show the tool is unchanged
options.B: Follow-up of every dealing the tool flags in Arabic minutes
options.C: Machine translation of the minutes into English before using the tool
options.D: Testing on Arabic minutes whose dealings are already known

questions.key_concept: An audit AI tool's validation applies only to data like that tested; a new language or data type needs revalidation before reliance.
questions.pre_read: Compare the data the tool was validated on with the data it will now read.
questions.correct_explanation: A validation holds only for data like the data tested. Unlike a fixed audit program, an AI tool's accuracy shifts with the data it reads, and Arabic minutes differ in language, wording and layout, so error rates on them are unknown until it is tested on Arabic minutes with known answers. Translating into English seems to reuse the validation, but translation adds its own errors, and the tool was never validated on translated text either.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because an unchanged audit program keeps its earlier testing. But an AI tool's accuracy depends on the data it reads; English results say nothing about Arabic minutes.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because flags get checked. But follow-up finds false flags only; dealings the tool misses in Arabic are never seen.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it routes minutes to the validated setting. But translation adds errors, and the tool was never validated on translated text.

tips: Eliminate: A retests the unchanged tool on English, which says nothing about Arabic, and B checks flags while misses go unseen.
Final two: D beats C because translation adds its own errors; only known-answer testing on Arabic minutes shows how the tool performs.
Exam cue: an AI audit tool's validation covers the data it was tested on. New languages, formats or sources need revalidation.

questions.subtopic: 3D Data quality and analytics. Anomaly tool reliance
questions.question: An audit team wants to rely on an anomaly-detection tool for a Botswanan trucking firm's fuel-card transactions, but no past cases with known answers exist. Which approach BEST supports that reliance?

options.A: Run the tool and follow up every transaction it flags
options.B: Run a second anomaly tool and compare the two sets of flags
options.C: Plant synthetic anomalies in a data copy and measure what is found
options.D: Rely on the detection rate the tool's vendor reports for fuel-card fraud

questions.key_concept: When no known-outcome data exists, seeded synthetic anomalies let the auditor measure an AI tool's miss rate before relying on it.
questions.pre_read: Ask how the team could learn what the tool misses.
questions.correct_explanation: Validation needs cases whose answers are known. When none exist, planting realistic synthetic anomalies in a copy of the data creates them, and the share the tool finds estimates its miss rate. Following up every flag is necessary, but it measures only false alarms; anomalies the tool never flags stay invisible, so it cannot show how far the tool can be relied on.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because every flag gets tested. But follow-up reveals false alarms only; anomalies the tool misses are never seen.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because two tools seem to check each other. But tools can share blind spots; agreement is not a measured miss rate.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because vendor figures sound objective. But they come from other data, not this firm's fuel-card transactions.

tips: Eliminate: D relies on vendor figures from other data, and B treats agreement between tools as accuracy.
Final two: C beats A because planted anomalies reveal what the tool misses; following up flags shows only its false alarms.
Exam cue: if no known outcomes exist, create them. Seeded test cases let the auditor measure an AI tool's misses before relying on it.

questions.subtopic: 3D Data quality and analytics. AI platform in an investigation
questions.question: Investigating suspected procurement fraud in a Trinidadian ministry's IT unit, the IS audit team may use that unit's AI platform, which keeps no copy of analyzed emails. What is the GREATEST concern?

options.A: The platform runs an open-source model rather than a major vendor's
options.B: Platform administrators can see the team's prompts and outputs
options.C: The platform's model has not been validated for analyzing emails
options.D: The platform's model is smaller than the leading public models

questions.key_concept: AI platforms log prompts and outputs; using one the auditee controls can expose confidential audit work and undermine independence.
questions.pre_read: Ask who runs the platform and what they could see.
questions.correct_explanation: AI platforms log prompts and outputs, and their administrators can usually read them. Keeping no copy of the emails does not change that. Here the administrators work in the unit under investigation, so they could see which people and payments the auditors are examining, defeating the investigation's confidentiality and independence. Validation matters before relying on any tool, but it cannot fix who runs the platform.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because some assume open-source models are less trustworthy. But a model's origin does not decide reliability; validation and who controls the platform do.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because an unvalidated tool is unreliable. But validation could be arranged; testing cannot fix a platform run by the people under investigation.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because bigger models often perform better. But size does not decide fitness for this task, and it does not touch the confidentiality problem.

tips: Eliminate: A judges the model by its origin and D by its size; neither decides reliability or confidentiality.
Final two: B beats C because testing could fix an unvalidated model, but not operators under investigation who can see the auditors' prompts.
Exam cue: an AI tool's prompt logs reveal what the auditor is examining. Keep confidential audit work off platforms the auditee controls.

questions.subtopic: 3D Data quality and analytics. A rerun that differs
questions.question: An IS auditor reran last year's AI extraction of refund amounts from 4,000 letters using recorded settings, prompts and input; 3% differ, as the vendor retired the original version. What should the auditor do FIRST?

options.A: Ask the vendor to restore the retired version for one rerun
options.B: Replace last year's amounts with the newer version's results
options.C: Keep last year's amounts and document the recorded run conditions
options.D: Check the differing amounts against the source and record the results

questions.key_concept: Recorded conditions make an AI rerun explainable, not guaranteed; when results differ, the auditor verifies against source records.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the records explain and what only the source data can settle.
questions.correct_explanation: Hosted models change, so even a well-recorded rerun can differ. The records explain why, a different version, but not which amounts are right. Checking the differing amounts against the source letters shows whether last year's results held, and recording that outcome settles the question. Keeping last year's amounts because conditions were recorded mistakes documentation for verification: recording makes a difference explainable, not correct.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the old version would reproduce the original. But vendors seldom restore retired versions, and a matching rerun still would not show the amounts are right.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the newer version is current. But it is a different model, and its amounts are no more verified than last year's.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because recording conditions is good practice. But records explain why results differ; only the source letters show which amounts are right.

tips: Eliminate: B swaps one unverified result for another, and A depends on the vendor reviving a retired version.
Final two: D beats C because recorded conditions explain a difference but cannot settle it; the source letters can.
Exam cue: hosted AI cannot always be rerun exactly. When a rerun differs, go back to the source records rather than to either output.

questions.subtopic: 3E Outputs and reports. Recommending on a biased model
questions.question: An IS auditor finds that an Austrian bank's voice-authentication model locks out customers with speech impairments far more often than other customers. Which recommendation is BEST?

options.A: Have the model owner set group lockout limits and fix any breach
options.B: Have the model owner raise the model's overall accuracy target
options.C: Retrain the model on 2,000 hours of speech from affected customers
options.D: Tell customers in the app that voice checks may sometimes fail

questions.key_concept: AI recommendations set group-level outcomes for a named owner; overall accuracy targets can hide a small group's harm, and owners choose the fix.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether each proposed measure would reveal the affected group's results, and who designs the fix.
questions.correct_explanation: An overall accuracy figure is dominated by the largest group, so a higher target can be met while customers with speech impairments stay locked out. Lockout limits for each group, owned and acted on by the model owner, make the gap visible and hold someone to closing it. The auditor recommends that outcome and its owner; the owner chooses the technical fix.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because better accuracy sounds like the cure. But an average can rise while a small group's lockouts stay high, so the gap could persist unseen.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because more representative data often narrows such gaps. But designing the fix is the owner's job; the auditor recommends the result to achieve.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it is transparent. But a notice leaves affected customers locked out; it informs without fixing anything.

tips: Eliminate: C has the auditor designing the model fix, and D informs customers without reducing lockouts.
Final two: A beats B because an overall target can be met while one group stays locked out; group limits make the gap visible and owned.
Exam cue: AI recommendations name a measurable outcome for each affected group and an owner. Averages hide small groups, and the fix is the owner's.

questions.subtopic: 3E Outputs and reports. Reporting a wait-time gap
questions.question: A Welsh council's AI policy requires fairness criteria for every model, but its repair-priority model has none, and Welsh-language requests wait 40% longer. How should the IS auditor BEST report this?

options.A: Report the wait gap as a finding against an auditor-set limit
options.B: Report nothing until the model owner has set fairness criteria
options.C: Report the missing fairness criteria, with the wait gap as effect
options.D: Report the wait gap as unlawful discrimination against Welsh speakers

questions.key_concept: If required AI fairness criteria are missing, the auditor reports the policy breach with its effect; model owners, not auditors, set fairness thresholds.
questions.pre_read: Find the criterion that already exists and the one that is missing.
questions.correct_explanation: The policy is the criterion, and the condition is that the model has no fairness criteria. With no limit to measure it against, the 40% gap cannot be called a breach, but it shows what the missing control allows: the effect on Welsh-language residents. Setting a limit and reporting a breach would have the auditor define the model's fairness threshold, a job for the model owner within senior management's tolerances.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because a finding against a number looks concrete. But turning fairness into a measurable limit is the model owner's job; an auditor-set limit would impair independence.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because there is no threshold to measure against. But the policy itself is the criterion, and its breach is reportable now.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the gap affects one language group. But unlawfulness is a legal judgment; the auditor reports facts against criteria and can refer possible breaches of language duties to counsel.

tips: Eliminate: B waits for criteria when the policy already supplies one, and D reaches a legal conclusion the auditor cannot make.
Final two: C beats A because the missing criteria breach the policy; setting a limit for the model would put the auditor in the model owner's role.
Exam cue: when an AI model lacks required criteria, report the governance gap against policy. Setting the model's fairness threshold is the model owner's job, not the auditor's.

questions.subtopic: 3E Outputs and reports. Explaining a model metric
questions.question: An IS auditor must explain to the audit committee that a Nepali health ministry's tuberculosis screening model has a false-negative rate three times higher in mountain districts. Which presentation is BEST?

options.A: How many healthy people it wrongly flags in mountain districts
options.B: How many sick people it likely misses, and the consequences
options.C: The model's overall accuracy across every district
options.D: The retraining method the IS auditor would use to close the gap

questions.key_concept: Explain technical AI findings to boards in terms of harm: a false-negative rate becomes real cases missed and their consequences.
questions.pre_read: Translate the metric into what happens to people before choosing a format.
questions.correct_explanation: A false-negative rate means sick people the model fails to flag. Committee members act on consequences, so the auditor translates the rate into the estimated number of people missed in mountain districts and what follows for them, such as later treatment. An overall accuracy figure looks balanced, but it blends all districts and can hide the mountain districts' gap, the harm the finding is about.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because wrong flags also harm people. But those are false positives; a false negative is a sick person the model fails to flag.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because an overall figure gives context. But it blends all districts, so it can hide the mountain districts' missed cases.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because a fix seems helpful. But designing the retraining is management's job, and the committee needs the risk, not a method.

tips: Eliminate: A describes false positives, not the false negatives in the finding, and D has the auditor designing the model fix.
Final two: B beats C because an overall figure blends all districts and can hide the gap; the committee needs the cases missed and what follows.
Exam cue: report AI metrics in terms of people and the business. A false-negative rate becomes the number of real cases missed.

questions.subtopic: 3E Outputs and reports. Closing a drift finding
questions.question: An IS auditor reported that a Latvian online retailer's returns-fraud model had no drift monitoring; at follow-up, management shows the retrained model is accurate again. What should the auditor do FIRST?

options.A: Accept the restored accuracy as evidence the drift finding is resolved
options.B: Retest accuracy on a sample of decisions since the retraining
options.C: Review the retrained model's validation report and monitoring plan
options.D: Verify that drift monitoring with alert limits and an owner now operates

questions.key_concept: Follow-up on an AI finding verifies that the missing control now operates; a retrained model's restored accuracy treats only the symptom.
questions.pre_read: Recall what the finding said was missing, then ask what management has shown.
questions.correct_explanation: The finding was missing drift monitoring; restored accuracy fixes the symptom, and drift can recur as customers' return patterns change. Follow-up verifies that the agreed control now operates: alert limits set, alerts reaching an owner and responses recorded. Retesting recent decisions is strong evidence of today's accuracy, but it does not show that the next decline will be detected.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the metric is back in range. But the cause was missing monitoring; without it, the next decline will again go unnoticed.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because production retests are strong follow-up evidence. But they show today's accuracy, the symptom; the finding was missing monitoring, which a retest does not examine.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it shows testing and intent. But a report and a plan show design; follow-up needs evidence that monitoring operates.

tips: Eliminate: A closes on a restored metric while the cause remains, and C offers a plan and a pre-release report, which show only design.
Final two: D beats B because the finding was missing monitoring; a production retest shows today's accuracy, not that the next decline will be caught.
Exam cue: follow-up tests what the finding reported. When it reported a missing control, retraining fixes only the symptom; close it when that control operates.

questions.subtopic: 3E Outputs and reports. Defending an AI-assisted finding
questions.question: Czech hospital managers dispute a finding that 312 overtime claims cover hours when badge records show staff off-site, calling the IS auditor's AI matching tool a black box. What is the auditor's BEST response?

options.A: Walk the managers through the badge and claim records for each item
options.B: Show the managers the vendor's accuracy certificate for the tool
options.C: Rerun the matching tool on the badge and claim records with managers
options.D: Withdraw the finding until the tool's method can be explained

questions.key_concept: AI tools find leads, but findings rest on source evidence the auditor verified and can show, so accountability stays with the auditor.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the finding actually rests on: the tool's output or the records behind it.
questions.correct_explanation: The tool found the leads, but the finding rests on records: the badge logs and the overtime claims for each item. Walking managers through that evidence shows the conclusion is the auditor's, supported by sources they can check, with no need to explain the tool's inner workings. Rerunning the tool shows only that it repeats itself; consistency does not show the claims are wrong.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because certificates sound authoritative. But a vendor's claim about the tool does not show these 312 claims are wrong.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because a repeated result looks convincing. But it shows the tool is consistent, not that its matches are right.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because unexplained AI output is weak evidence. But this finding rests on badge and claim records the auditor can show, not on the tool.

tips: Eliminate: B offers a vendor claim instead of evidence, and D withdraws a finding that rests on records rather than on the tool.
Final two: A beats C because the auditor owns the conclusion through the source records; a rerun shows only that the tool repeats itself.
Exam cue: when AI found it, the evidence must still stand without the AI. Defend findings with source records, not with the tool.

options.B: An AI search tool that gathered public news about the auditee
options.C: An AI tool that chose which transactions the auditors would test
options.D: An AI tool that translated auditee policies the auditors read for context

A tool that chose which transactions to test set the audit's coverage and evidence, so readers need to know how it was used, validated and checked by the auditors. Gathering public news informs background research for planning, but no finding rests on it, so it matters far less to readers.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it fed the risk assessment. But background news informs planning; no finding rests on it the way findings rest on test selection.

tips: Eliminate: A polishes wording and D translated background reading; neither shapes the evidence behind the findings.

questions.subtopic: 3A Audit planning and design. A vendor-enabled AI feature
questions.question: Mid-year, a Manitoba credit union's core banking vendor switches on a built-in AI feature that sends members' overdue loans to collectors. What should the IS audit manager do FIRST?

options.A: Add the feature to the audit universe at next year's annual refresh
options.B: Recommend that IT switch the feature off until it is audited
options.C: Add the feature to the audit universe and re-rank this year's plan
options.D: Swap the plan's lowest-ranked audit for an audit of the feature

questions.key_concept: Embedded AI switched on by a vendor changes the audit universe mid-cycle; add it and re-rank the plan by likelihood and impact.
questions.pre_read: Notice who switched the feature on and what it now decides about people.
questions.correct_explanation: A vendor can switch on embedded AI without any project, so the risk profile changes mid-cycle. The feature now decides which members are sent to collectors, so the manager adds it to the audit universe and re-ranks the plan by the likelihood and impact of harm to members and the credit union. Swapping out the lowest-ranked audit skips that ranking: the feature may not outrank that audit, or may outrank several.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because universes are refreshed on a cycle. But embedded AI switched on mid-year already decides about members; waiting a year leaves it unranked.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the feature is unaudited. But no risk has been assessed yet, so a shutdown has no evidence behind it; an audit is not a precondition for use.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it acts fast. But the swap assumes the feature's rank; only re-ranking by likelihood and impact shows what it should displace.

tips: Eliminate: A waits for the annual cycle while the feature already sends members to collectors, and B recommends a shutdown before any risk has been assessed.
Final two: C beats D because re-ranking by likelihood and impact shows where the feature belongs; a swap assumes the answer before the ranking is done.
Exam cue: when a vendor switches on embedded AI mid-cycle, update the audit universe and re-rank now. Audit effort follows ranked risk, not the order uses appeared.

questions.subtopic: 3A Audit planning and design. Inventory entry for an AI platform
questions.question: A Bermudian insurer's AI inventory lists its generative AI platform as one medium-risk entry, though staff built 25 assistants on it, from meeting-note summaries to claim-denial letters. What should the IS audit manager do FIRST?

options.A: Add each assistant to the audit universe, ranked by its use
options.B: Plan one platform audit of the shared controls behind the assistants
options.C: Keep the medium rating, since the platform passed a risk review
options.D: Rate the platform high, since generative AI is a new technology

questions.key_concept: AI risk sits in each use; uses built on one shared platform are listed and ranked separately in the audit universe.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether one inventory entry can carry one risk rating for everything built on it.
questions.correct_explanation: Risk in generative AI sits in each use, not in the platform: the same model is low risk summarizing meeting notes and high risk drafting claim denials. Adding each assistant to the audit universe lets the manager rank each by the likelihood and impact of harm to claimants and the insurer. A platform audit planned before that ranking tests shared controls, not how denial drafts are reviewed.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the platform is shared infrastructure. But platform controls say nothing about each assistant's use, such as how denial drafts are checked.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because a review exists. But one platform-wide rating hides the different risks of its 25 uses, from note summaries to claim denials.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because generative AI feels risky. But novelty is not risk; ranking follows the likelihood and impact of each use.

tips: Eliminate: C lets one platform-wide rating stand for 25 different uses, and D ranks by novelty instead of likelihood and impact.
Final two: A beats B because ranking comes before planning; a platform audit tests shared controls but not how a claim-denial draft reaches claimants.
Exam cue: a shared AI platform is not one risk. List and rank each use built on it, because the use sets the impact.

questions.subtopic: 3A Audit planning and design. Scoping a retrieval assistant
questions.question: A Seychelles port's AI assistant answers shipping agents from its library of tariff notices, revised monthly, and the IS auditor's draft scope covers answer accuracy, hosting and the vendor contract. Which addition is MOST needed?

options.A: Penetration testing of the assistant's public web page
options.B: The wording of the disclaimer shown under each tariff answer
options.C: Prompt rules that make the assistant cite each notice and its date
options.D: How the source tariff notices are approved, updated and retired

questions.key_concept: A retrieval-based assistant answers from its document library, so scope covers how those documents are approved, updated and retired.
questions.pre_read: Find where the assistant's answers come from before deciding what the scope misses.
questions.correct_explanation: The assistant answers from retrieved documents, so a superseded or unapproved notice in the library produces a confident, wrong tariff answer however good the model is. Scoping how notices are approved, updated and retired covers where much of this risk sits. A cited notice and its date help agents trace an answer, but a date cannot show that the notice has since been superseded, so citing it cannot keep the library current.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because public web pages attract attacks. But hosting is already in scope, and a penetration test says nothing about whether answers rest on current notices.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because a disclaimer warns agents to check. But it shifts the check onto agents and does nothing to keep the library's notices current.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because a notice and its date let agents trace each answer. But a date shows when a notice was issued, not whether it has since been superseded.

tips: Eliminate: A tests the web page's security, which says nothing about the notices behind each answer, and B treats a disclaimer as if it controlled the answers.
Final two: D beats C because a citation and date show which notice an answer used, not whether it is still current.
Exam cue: for a retrieval-based assistant, scope how the source library is approved and updated. Stale or unapproved documents produce confident wrong answers.

questions.subtopic: 3A Audit planning and design. A requested scope exclusion
questions.question: An IS auditor scoping a Kosovo car-sharing firm's reckless-driving ban model is asked by the sponsor to exclude appeals, the only human review of a ban, as outside the model. What is the BEST response?

options.A: Exclude appeals and record the exclusion and its reason in the plan
options.B: Keep appeals in the audit as part of the AI decision process
options.C: Leave appeals to a later audit of the member services function
options.D: Include appeals if complaint volumes pass an agreed threshold

questions.key_concept: An AI audit's scope covers the decision process around the model, including appeals, even when they sit outside the model.
questions.pre_read: Ask what protects a member the model bans wrongly, and who tests it.
questions.correct_explanation: Appeals are part of the AI decision process: they are how a member wrongly banned for reckless driving gets a person to review the decision. Sitting outside the model does not move them out of scope. Recording an exclusion fits a limitation the auditor cannot avoid, but this one removes the only human review, so the auditor keeps appeals in scope and escalates to the audit committee if the sponsor insists.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because documenting exclusions is good practice. But an AI audit that skips the appeal route cannot conclude on oversight of decisions that ban members from the service.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because member services has its own audits. But a later audit separates the safeguard from the model it protects, leaving this conclusion incomplete.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it sounds risk-based. But complaint volume shows who complained, not whether appeals work for members wrongly banned.

tips: Eliminate: C splits the safeguard from the model it protects, and D lets complaint volume decide scope instead of the decision process.
Final two: B beats A because the appeal route is part of the AI decision process; documenting its exclusion still leaves oversight of bans untested.
Exam cue: scope an AI decision end to end, including review, override and appeal. A step outside the model is still inside the AI audit.

questions.subtopic: 3A Audit planning and design. Invitation to a design team
questions.question: A Lesotho garment maker's data science team invites the IS auditor onto the design team for a new shift-scheduling model, to build in auditability. What is the auditor's BEST response?

options.A: Advise on the logs and version records the model should keep
options.B: Serve as the model's independent validator before launch
options.C: Join the team and pick input features that avoid bias
options.D: Decline to meet the team until the model goes live

questions.key_concept: The IS auditor may advise an AI design team on the evidence a model should keep, but never designs, validates or approves the model.
questions.pre_read: Separate advice about evidence from decisions about how the model works.
questions.correct_explanation: IS auditors may advise on what evidence a model should leave, such as decision logs, model versions and data lineage, without making design choices. That builds in auditability and keeps the auditor free to audit the model later. Acting as its independent validator sounds like assurance, but validation is a control management runs before launch; an auditor who performed it would later be auditing their own work.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because validators must be independent of the builders. But validation is part of management's control system; performing it would have the auditor later reviewing their own work.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because avoiding bias matters. But choosing features is a design decision; the auditor would then audit their own work.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it protects independence. But auditors can advise early on evidence needs; refusing contact loses the chance to build in an audit trail.

tips: Eliminate: C makes the auditor a designer of the model, and D gives up early advice that independence allows.
Final two: A beats B because advising on evidence leaves every decision with management; validating the model makes the auditor perform a control they must later audit.
Exam cue: early in an AI project, the auditor advises on the evidence the model must keep. Designing, validating or approving the model belongs to management.

questions.subtopic: 3A Audit planning and design. Using a validation unit's work
questions.question: A Puerto Rican staffing agency's validation unit, independent of the builders, reported only overall accuracy for its pay-offer model, and IS audit lacks machine-learning skills. How should the IS audit manager BEST use this work?

options.A: Rely on the unit's report, since validators were independent of builders
options.B: Have a co-sourced specialist repeat the unit's accuracy tests
options.C: Use it for accuracy and co-source tests of pay offers by group
options.D: Ask the builders whether validation covered the pay-offer model's main risks

questions.key_concept: Independent validation can be used for what it tested; the audit fills gaps, such as group fairness, that one accuracy figure cannot show.
questions.pre_read: List what the validation measured, then ask what risk of this model it leaves untested.
questions.correct_explanation: Independent validation can be relied on for what it tested, once the manager has evaluated the unit's competence and method. One overall accuracy figure says nothing about whether pay offers differ unfairly across worker groups, so the manager uses the work for accuracy and fills the gap with a co-sourced specialist. Relying on the report for everything treats independence as coverage; independent work still covers only what it tested.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the validators are independent of the builders. But independence shows objectivity, not coverage; an overall accuracy figure cannot show fair pay offers across groups.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it uses a specialist. But repeating the same accuracy tests duplicates covered work and still leaves pay offers by group untested.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the builders know the model. But they are the subject of the validation; their view of its coverage is not independent evidence.

tips: Eliminate: B repeats work the unit already covered, and D asks the builders to vouch for a review of their own model.
Final two: C beats A because independence makes the unit's work usable, not complete; overall accuracy cannot show whether pay offers are fair across worker groups.
Exam cue: when using others' AI testing, rely on what it covered and fill the gaps. An overall accuracy figure never answers the fairness question.

questions.subtopic: 3A Audit planning and design. An audit tool for sample selection
questions.question: An Andorran ski-lift operator's audit methodology approves an AI tool for summarizing auditee policies; a senior IS auditor wants it to choose which supplier payments to test. What should the IS audit manager do FIRST?

options.A: Allow the use, since the methodology already approves the tool
options.B: Treat choosing samples as a new use to assess and approve
options.C: Let the auditor use it, then review the payments it picks
options.D: Save the prompts used so the selection can be rerun later

questions.key_concept: Audit AI tools are approved for specific uses; a higher-risk new use, such as choosing samples, needs its own assessment and approval.
questions.pre_read: Compare what the tool was approved for with what it would now decide.
questions.correct_explanation: Approval is for a use, not a tool. Summarizing policies is low risk; choosing the sample decides what the audit tests, and a tool's selection can skew coverage in ways nobody can explain. So the new use needs its own risk assessment, approval and validation before it shapes an engagement. Reviewing the picks afterward checks the payments chosen, not the payments the tool left out.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the tool is approved. But approval covered summarizing policies; selecting samples carries different risks to coverage and explainability.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because review is a control. But reviewing chosen payments cannot reveal what the selection skipped; the use needs approval before it shapes testing.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because reruns support review. But saving prompts documents an unapproved use; it does not decide whether the tool may choose samples.

tips: Eliminate: A stretches an approval beyond the use it covered, and D documents the selection without deciding whether it is allowed.
Final two: B beats C because sample selection decides what gets tested; reviewing the tool's picks afterward cannot show what it left out.
Exam cue: audit AI approvals are per use. A new task for an approved tool, especially one that shapes testing, is assessed and approved first.

questions.subtopic: 3A Audit planning and design. Version retirement and audit tools
questions.question: A Bahamian trust company's chief audit executive is weighing a hosted AI tool for audit testing, but its vendor retires versions yearly and regulators may revisit work for five years. Which requirement is BEST?

options.A: Contract the vendor to keep retired versions available for five years
options.B: Rerun tests on the newest version whenever regulators revisit them
options.C: Bar the tool from any test that regulators might revisit
options.D: Keep each output with its run conditions and source checks

questions.key_concept: Hosted AI cannot guarantee identical reruns, so audit work papers keep outputs, run conditions and source checks that stand without a rerun.
questions.pre_read: Ask what a regulator could rely on in five years if the tool's version no longer exists.
questions.correct_explanation: Hosted models change and retire, and even a kept version may not rerun identically, so the work papers must stand without a rerun. Keeping each output with its recorded run conditions and the auditor's checks against source records lets a reviewer see what was done and why the conclusion holds. Contracting for retired versions helps a rerun, but cannot guarantee identical results and leaves the evidence resting on the tool.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because it seems to secure reruns. But hosted versions may not rerun identically even if kept; the evidence should rest on verified sources.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the newest version is supported. But a different version answers differently, so a rerun cannot show what the original test found.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it removes the problem. But it gives up the tool's benefits when recorded, source-checked work papers already meet the need.

tips: Eliminate: B reruns on a different model and calls it the same test, and C bans a use that good work papers can support.
Final two: D beats A because work papers that record conditions and source checks stand on their own; a kept version still may not rerun identically.
Exam cue: before approving a hosted AI tool for audit work, require work papers that stand without a rerun, with recorded conditions and source checks. Never plan on a vendor keeping a version alive.

questions.subtopic: 3B Testing and sampling. Builders' control list
questions.question: The data science team's control list for a Gambian airline's model, which overbooks flights it predicts will have no-shows, covers validation and drift monitoring. What should the IS auditor do FIRST?

options.A: Test the listed controls, since they span the model's lifecycle
options.B: Map the model's risks to controls independently of the list
options.C: Ask the team to confirm in writing that the list is complete
options.D: Check the model card for controls missing from the list

questions.key_concept: The IS auditor maps an AI model's risks to controls independently, rather than testing only the controls its builders describe.
questions.pre_read: Ask who wrote the control list and what risks they might not see.
questions.correct_explanation: Builders list the controls they run, and an AI model's risks reach beyond them: who can change training data, who approves retraining, whether staff can override an overbooking and how bumped passengers are affected. Mapping risks to controls independently shows which controls should exist before testing begins. Validation and drift monitoring are only two lifecycle stages; testing them alone lets the auditee define the audit.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because validation and drift monitoring sound like the whole lifecycle. But they skip training-data access, retraining approval and overrides; testing them alone lets builders set the audit's bounds.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it seems to close the gap. But a written confirmation from the team is still the team's own view of its controls.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because model cards describe the model. But the card is the builders' document too, so it shares the list's blind spots.

tips: Eliminate: C turns the team's own view into a signed statement, and D checks a document the same builders wrote.
Final two: B beats A because validation and drift monitoring are only two lifecycle stages; mapping risks first shows missing controls such as retraining approval.
Exam cue: never let builders' control lists set an AI audit's scope. Map risks to controls yourself, then test.

questions.subtopic: 3B Testing and sampling. A model switch-off control
questions.question: A Togolese social security fund's procedure lets its benefits manager switch off the family-allowance model and route applications to staff. Which evidence BEST shows the IS auditor that this control operates?

options.A: The documented switch-off procedure for routing applications to staff
options.B: A logged switch-off of the model in the test environment
options.C: A logged production switch-off, with the fallback then working
options.D: The vendor's description of the platform's switch-off feature

questions.key_concept: The power to stop an AI system is effective oversight only when a tested switch-off and the manual fallback both work.
questions.pre_read: Ask what must happen after the model is switched off for the control to work.
questions.correct_explanation: Stopping a model is a key oversight control only if it works end to end: the model stops in production, and staff then decide applications in its place. A logged production switch-off shows both. A switch-off in the test environment shows the model can stop, but not that the live fallback works or that staff can carry the real caseload without the model.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because procedures define the control. But a document shows design; it cannot show the switch-off and fallback ever worked.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it is a logged switch-off. But a test environment shows only that the model can stop, not that staff in production take over the applications.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the feature exists. But the vendor describes its product, not whether this fund's switch-off and fallback operate.

tips: Eliminate: A shows only the control's design, and D is the vendor's account of a feature rather than evidence of its use.
Final two: C beats B because the control works only if production stops and staff then decide; a test-environment stop never shows the fallback carrying real cases.
Exam cue: a person's power to stop an AI system counts only if the stop and the manual fallback both work. Look for a tested switch-off.

questions.subtopic: 3B Testing and sampling. Adding a stratum
questions.question: An IS auditor's sample of a Montenegrin probation service's supervision-level decisions is stratified by home region; officers override about 4% of the model's levels. Which added stratum BEST helps find the model's errors?

options.A: Levels set in the months when caseloads peaked last year
options.B: Levels the officers chose not to override, drawn at random
options.C: Levels for people who later complained about their level
options.D: Levels the officers overrode, with the model's original level

questions.key_concept: Human overrides mark where people judged an AI decision wrong, so an overrides stratum focuses testing on likely errors.
questions.pre_read: Ask where in the records the model's errors are most likely to show.
questions.correct_explanation: Overrides mark the levels a probation officer judged wrong, so they gather the model's likely errors; comparing each with the model's original level shows what it missed. An overrides stratum lets the auditor test those decisions directly, and check that the overrides themselves treat regions consistently. Complaints also point at errors, but only from people who chose to complain, and nobody complains about a level set too low.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because caseload peaks stress the service. But peaks raise volume, not the share of wrong levels; nothing points the model's errors there.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it widens coverage. But the stratified sample already draws from these levels; a random extra stratum adds no focus on errors.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because complaints signal wrong levels. But complainers are a self-selected few, and none object to a level set too low; overrides cover both.

tips: Eliminate: A adds caseload peaks, which raise volume rather than errors, and B adds a random draw of levels the main sample already covers.
Final two: D beats C because overrides record every level an officer judged wrong; complaints come only from people who speak up, never about levels set too low.
Exam cue: when sampling AI decisions, add strata where errors gather, such as human overrides, low-confidence scores and recent model versions.

questions.subtopic: 3B Testing and sampling. Testing automatic approvals
questions.question: A Beninese cotton board's model auto-approves farmers' input-subsidy claims with risk scores below 0.2 and sends the rest to officers. Which population BEST supports the IS auditor's test of whether auto-approval works?

options.A: Auto-approved claims, each checked against farm and delivery records
options.B: Claims officers reviewed, compared with their final decisions
options.C: Claims later found fraudulent, traced back to their model scores
options.D: Past claims with known outcomes, rescored by the current model

questions.key_concept: To test automated approval, sample the auto-approved items against independent records; known failures exclude everything nobody detected.
questions.pre_read: Find the decisions no person reviews, and ask where their errors would show.
questions.correct_explanation: Auto-approval is the part no person checks, so its effectiveness shows only in auto-approved claims tested against independent records. Claims later found fraudulent are useful, but they are only the cases someone happened to detect; fraud inside auto-approved claims that nobody caught never reaches that list. Officer-reviewed claims test the referral path, not auto-approval.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because officer decisions are a ready check. But referred claims show how risky cases are handled, not what auto-approval let through.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because they are confirmed errors. But detected fraud is only the fraud someone caught; undetected cases in auto-approved claims stay outside it.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because outcomes are known. But past claims rescored today test the current model on old data, not what auto-approval did this year.

tips: Eliminate: B tests the path officers already review, and D rescores old claims rather than testing this year's approvals.
Final two: A beats C because detected fraud includes only what someone caught; testing auto-approved claims against records can find what nobody caught.
Exam cue: to test an automated decision, sample what it decided without a person. Known failures are leads, never the full population.

questions.subtopic: 3B Testing and sampling. Reperforming from a feature store
questions.question: To reperform a Bruneian buy-now-pay-later provider's spending-limit renewals, the IS auditor plans to pull sampled customers' features from the feature store and score them with the archived version that decided. What is the GREATEST concern?

options.A: The store may hold today's values, not those used when deciding
options.B: The archived version may not read the store's current feature format
options.C: The sample may hold too few large limit cuts to compare groups
options.D: The archived version differs from the model now in production

questions.key_concept: Reperformance needs the deciding model version and the inputs as they were at decision time; current feature values change the case.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether each input to the rerun is what the model saw on the day it decided.
questions.correct_explanation: Reperforming a decision needs the model version that made it and the inputs as they were then. A feature store often keeps each customer's latest values, such as missed repayments and monthly spending, so today's features would have the archived version score a different case. The rerun could then disagree, or agree, for the wrong reason, with nothing to warn the auditor. A format mismatch fails visibly and can be fixed.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because feature formats change over time. But a format mismatch fails visibly and can be fixed; stale inputs fail silently and corrupt every comparison.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because group comparisons need enough cases. But the objective is reperforming decisions, not fairness; sample design does not fix wrong inputs.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because versions differ. But using the deciding version is the right choice; the current model would be the wrong one.

tips: Eliminate: D names the correct choice of model as a problem, and C raises a fairness question this test does not ask.
Final two: A beats B because current feature values silently change the case being scored; a format mismatch fails visibly.
Exam cue: reperforming an AI decision needs the deciding version and the inputs as they were then. Ask whether each input is a point-in-time record.

questions.subtopic: 3B Testing and sampling. Challenger model results
questions.question: An IS auditor's independently built challenger model disagrees with a Kazakh steel mill's scrap-grading model on 7% of 30,000 scrap loads. What should the auditor do FIRST?

options.A: Report the 7% disagreement as the grading model's error rate
options.B: Treat the loads where both models agree as correctly graded
options.C: Recommend retraining the grading model on the challenger's grades
options.D: Check a sample of disagreeing loads against independent expert grades

questions.key_concept: A challenger model's disagreements are leads; the auditor verifies a sample against an independent source before measuring errors.
questions.pre_read: Ask which source, other than either model, shows the right grade.
questions.correct_explanation: A challenger model is another model, not the truth. Disagreements show where one of the two is likely wrong, so they are leads: checking a sample against independent expert grades shows which model erred and how often. Reporting 7% as the grading model's error rate assumes the challenger is right every time, when it may be the one making the mistakes.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the challenger was built independently. But independence is not accuracy; until disagreements are checked, the 7% could be the challenger's errors.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because agreement feels like confirmation. But two models trained on similar data can share the same errors.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it seems to fix the gap. But retraining design belongs to the model owner, and the challenger's grades are unverified.

tips: Eliminate: B treats agreement between two models as proof, and C has the auditor steering the owner's model fix.
Final two: D beats A because a challenger's disagreement is a lead; only independent expert grades show which model graded each load wrongly.
Exam cue: an audit challenger model points testing at likely errors. Its outputs are leads to verify, not a measure of the production model's accuracy.

questions.subtopic: 3C Evidence collection. Evidence of a threshold change
questions.question: A Sierra Leonean energy agency's solar-rebate approvals halved in June; its screening model's version log shows no release since January. Which evidence BEST shows the IS auditor whether, and by whom, the cutoff was altered?

options.A: The model card's stated cutoff score for rebate approvals
options.B: June's decision log showing each applicant's score and outcome
options.C: The scoring platform's settings history for the cutoff value
options.D: The model version log naming who approved each release

questions.key_concept: AI thresholds are configuration that can change without a new model version; settings history, not the version log, shows such changes.
questions.pre_read: Separate what the trained model holds from what is set around it.
questions.correct_explanation: A cutoff is usually a platform setting rather than part of the trained model, so it can be altered without a new model version. The platform's settings history for that value shows whether, when and by whom the cutoff moved. June's decision log lets the auditor infer an effective cutoff from scores and outcomes, but cannot prove the setting was altered, or show who altered it.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because it states the cutoff. But a model card is the builders' description and may never have been updated after a settings change.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because scores and outcomes reveal the effective cutoff. But inference shows a pattern, not the change itself, when it happened or who made it.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it records approvers and shows no release since January. But a cutoff set on the platform can move without a new version, so this log cannot show it.

tips: Eliminate: A is the builders' description, which may predate any change, and D records model releases, while a platform cutoff can move without one.
Final two: C beats B because the settings history records the change itself; decision logs only let the auditor infer one.
Exam cue: a model's threshold can change without a new version. Ask for the configuration history, not just the model version log.

questions.subtopic: 3C Evidence collection. Use beyond validated limits
questions.question: A Quebec dental chain's cavity-detection model card says it was validated on adult X-rays only. Which evidence BEST shows the IS auditor whether the model is used beyond that limit?

options.A: The validation report describing the X-rays in its test data
options.B: Production scan logs recording each patient's age band
options.C: Booking rules that send children to dentists not using the model
options.D: The clinical lead's statement on which patients the model reads

questions.key_concept: Whether an AI model is used beyond its validated limits shows in production records, compared with the model card's stated limits.
questions.pre_read: Ask which record shows whose X-rays the model actually read.
questions.correct_explanation: The question is how the model is actually used, so the evidence is production records of whose X-rays it read. Scan logs with each patient's age band show whether children's X-rays went through the model despite the adult-only validation. Booking rules show a control's design, but bookings change and walk-ins happen, so rules cannot show which X-rays the model really read.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because it defines the validated population. But it shows which X-rays were tested before release, not which the model reads now.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it looks like a preventive control. But a rule shows design; only production records show whose X-rays actually reached the model.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the clinical lead knows the practice. But a statement of intended use is inquiry, the weakest evidence of actual use.

tips: Eliminate: A shows what was tested before release, and D is a person's account rather than a record of use.
Final two: B beats C because scan logs show whose X-rays the model read; booking rules show only how use was meant to be limited.
Exam cue: to check use against a model card's limits, compare the card with production records. Rules and intentions show design, not use.

questions.subtopic: 3C Evidence collection. Evidence of retraining approval
questions.question: A Djiboutian bank's trade-finance fraud model can be retrained and promoted to production automatically by its pipeline. Which evidence BEST shows the IS auditor that every retrained version was approved before use?

options.A: Inquiry of the model owner about the approval steps
options.B: A walkthrough of the next planned retraining and its approval
options.C: The pipeline's gate that blocks promotion unless validation tests pass
options.D: The model registry's version history, matched to approvals

questions.key_concept: Pipelines can promote retrained models with no human sign-off; match the registry's version history to approvals, since passing the builders' test gate is not approval.
questions.pre_read: Separate a pipeline checking metrics from a person approving a model.
questions.correct_explanation: When a pipeline can promote models by itself, the question is whether someone with authority approved each version before it went live. The model registry is where the pipeline records each version it promotes, so matching its history to approval records tests the whole period. A validation gate shows the pipeline checks builders' metrics; passing those tests is not the owner's approval, and the gate's design says nothing about versions already promoted.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the owner knows the process. But inquiry is the weakest evidence and cannot show what the pipeline did on its own.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it observes the process. But one walkthrough shows a single future event, not whether every past version was approved.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because an automated preventive control looks strong. But passing builders' validation tests is not an owner's approval, and the gate's design shows nothing about past versions.

tips: Eliminate: A rests on inquiry alone, and B observes one future retrain rather than the period under audit.
Final two: D beats C because approval is a person accepting each version; a gate that checks metrics is the builders' test, and its design shows nothing about past promotions.
Exam cue: when AI pipelines retrain and deploy on their own, test approval across the model registry's history. A passed test gate is not an approval.

questions.subtopic: 3C Evidence collection. Records of an agent's actions
questions.question: To test which customer accounts an Eswatini electricity company's AI agent changed, the IS auditor is offered the agent's own end-of-day summaries of its actions. Which evidence is MOST reliable?

options.A: The billing system's audit trail of changes by the agent's account
options.B: The agent's summaries, checked by asking it to relist its changes
options.C: The supervisor's daily sign-off on each of the agent's summaries
options.D: The permissions configured for the agent's customer account changes

questions.key_concept: An AI agent's summaries of its own actions are self-reports; the target system's audit trail is the reliable record.
questions.pre_read: Ask who produced each record: the agent, a person reading the agent, or the system acted on.
questions.correct_explanation: An agent's summary is its own account of what it did, and generated text can omit or misstate actions. The billing system's audit trail records every change made under the agent's account, independent of what the agent says. A supervisor's sign-off adds a review, but the supervisor signs the same self-report and has no independent record to compare it with.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it seems to double-check. But asking the agent again tests its consistency, not its accuracy; it can repeat the same omissions.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because management review is a control. But the supervisor reviews the agent's self-report, so the sign-off inherits its gaps.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because permissions bound the agent. But they show what it could change, not what it actually changed.

tips: Eliminate: B asks the agent to check itself, and D shows what the agent could change rather than what it did.
Final two: A beats C because the system's audit trail records changes independently; a supervisor signing the agent's summary still relies on the agent's own account.
Exam cue: an AI agent's report of its own actions is a lead. The record of what it did lives in the systems it acted on.

questions.subtopic: 3C Evidence collection. Checking an AI summary
questions.question: An IS auditor confirmed that every statement in an approved AI tool's summary of a Timor-Leste ministry's 90-page IT risk register appears in the register. What is the GREATEST remaining concern?

options.A: A rerun of the same prompt might give a different summary
options.B: The summary might leave out risks the register rates high
options.C: The vendor might keep the register to train its models
options.D: The tool's confidence score for the summary was not recorded

questions.key_concept: Tracing an AI summary's statements to the source catches invented content but not omissions; check important source items against the summary too.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the check performed can and cannot detect.
questions.correct_explanation: Tracing each statement to the register tests what the summary says, so invented content is ruled out. It cannot test what the summary left out, and summarizing tools often drop items, including high-rated risks the audit plan depends on. Comparing the register's high-rated risks with the summary closes that gap. A rerun that differs is a reproducibility issue; it does not show this summary is incomplete.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because reruns can vary. But variation is handled by recording run conditions; it says nothing about whether this summary omitted risks.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because audit data must stay confidential. But the tool is approved, so its data terms were already assessed.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because confidence feels like quality. But a tool's self-rating is not evidence, and recording it would not reveal omissions.

tips: Eliminate: C reopens data terms the tool's approval already covered, and D relies on the tool's rating of itself.
Final two: B beats A because tracing statements catches inventions, not omissions; a summary can be accurate in every line and still drop key risks.
Exam cue: verify AI output both ways: is each statement in the source, and is each important source item in the output?

questions.subtopic: 3C Evidence collection. An auditee's AI-produced review
questions.question: A Bavarian auto-parts maker's IT team says its AI assistant reviewed all 1,200 access changes this year against approvals and found no exceptions. What should the IS auditor do FIRST?

options.A: Rely on the assistant's review of the 1,200 access changes against approvals
options.B: Ask the assistant's vendor for its published accuracy rate
options.C: Test a sample of the access changes against approvals directly
options.D: Rerun the team's assistant on the changes with the auditor's own prompts

questions.key_concept: An auditee's AI-produced control review is management's assertion; the auditor obtains direct evidence by testing the underlying records.
questions.pre_read: Ask who ran the tool and whose conclusion its result is.
questions.correct_explanation: The assistant's result is the IT team's own review, produced with a tool the auditee runs and prompts, so it is management's assertion, not the auditor's own evidence. Testing a sample of access changes against approvals gives the auditor direct evidence. Rerunning the assistant with the auditor's own prompts feels independent, but the auditee's unvalidated tool would still judge each change.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because full coverage sounds strong. But the review was run by the auditee with its own tool; coverage claimed is not coverage tested.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because accuracy matters. But a vendor's figure comes from other data and says nothing about this review.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the auditor writes the prompts. But the auditee's unvalidated assistant still judges each change; rerunning it does not show those judgments are right.

tips: Eliminate: A accepts the auditee's own claim of full coverage, and B relies on a vendor figure from other data.
Final two: C beats D because testing changes against approvals gives the auditor direct evidence; rerunning the auditee's unvalidated assistant still relies on its judgment.
Exam cue: an auditee's AI-produced review is a management assertion. Test the underlying records; rerunning the auditee's tool, even with new prompts, only repeats its judgments.

questions.subtopic: 3D Data quality and analytics. Model-replaced values in audit data
questions.question: Recomputing a Surinamese ministry's childcare-subsidy approval rates by stated income band, an IS auditor learns a data-warehouse cleaning model judged 18% of incomes implausible and replaced them with estimates. What should the auditor do FIRST?

options.A: Exclude the 18% with estimated incomes from the recomputation
options.B: Use the extract, since the data team validated its cleaning model
options.C: Obtain the incomes applicants stated from the application system
options.D: Ask the data team to document why stated incomes were replaced

questions.key_concept: Values a model imputed or replaced are estimates, not source records; the auditor obtains source values rather than testing or dropping estimates.
questions.pre_read: Ask which values in the extract came from people and which came from a model.
questions.correct_explanation: A model's estimates are not source data: replaced incomes show what a cleaning model guessed, not what applicants stated, so they can move people between income bands. The auditor goes back to the application system for the recorded incomes. Excluding the 18% looks cautious, but values judged implausible may cluster among some applicants, such as the self-employed, so dropping them can distort the very rates being compared.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because it avoids estimated values. But the replaced records may not be random, so dropping them can skew approval rates by band.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the cleaning model was validated. But validation shows it estimates well on average, not that estimates equal each applicant's stated income.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because understanding the replacements helps. But documentation explains why values changed without restoring the incomes applicants stated.

tips: Eliminate: B treats a validated estimate as the recorded value, and D documents why values changed instead of restoring the source values.
Final two: C beats A because the source holds the stated incomes; dropping the replaced 18% can skew the income bands being compared.
Exam cue: when a model has filled in or replaced values in audit data, go back to the source. Model estimates are not records.

questions.subtopic: 3D Data quality and analytics. AI-written extract query
questions.question: An IS auditor's approved AI assistant wrote the query extracting a Belizean tourism board's tour-guide licensing decisions; the assistant then queried the source system for a total, which matched. What should the auditor do FIRST?

options.A: Compare the extract to a total from the system's own reports
options.B: Rely on the match, since the total came from the source system
options.C: Accept the extract, since the assistant is approved for audit use
options.D: Ask the assistant to explain what each of its queries does

questions.key_concept: A reconciliation is independent only if the source total comes from outside the AI tool that wrote the extract query.
questions.pre_read: Ask who produced each of the two numbers being compared.
questions.correct_explanation: The assistant wrote both queries, so the match checks its work against itself: an AI-written query can drop records through a wrong join, filter or date range, and the same misreading of the schema can shape the total too. A total the assistant did not produce, such as the system's own report, gives an independent check. A source-system figure is independent only when the query behind it is.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the total came from the source system. But the assistant wrote that query too, so one wrong filter or date range can shape both numbers.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the tool passed the audit function's approval. But approval permits using the tool; it does not show this query returned every record.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it seems to check the logic. But the assistant explaining its own queries can repeat its own mistake.

tips: Eliminate: C treats the tool's approval as proof of this one output, and D asks the tool to check its own work.
Final two: A beats B because a total the same assistant queried is not independent; one misread schema can drop the same records from both counts.
Exam cue: reconcile AI-written extracts to a figure the AI tool did not shape. A total the same assistant queried checks its work against itself.
