questions.subtopic: 3D Data quality and analytics. Scoring an audit tool
questions.question: A Faroese salmon exporter's audit team tuned its AI duplicate-invoice tool on 200 known duplicates, then reported it found 196 of them. What is the GREATEST concern with relying on this result?

options.A: Two hundred known duplicates are too few to tune the tool
options.B: The tool may also flag many invoices that are not duplicates
options.C: The tool vendor's own published accuracy figure was not checked
options.D: The tool was scored on the same cases used to tune it

questions.key_concept: An audit AI tool scored on the cases used to tune it overstates performance; validation needs known cases held back from tuning.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether the tool had already seen the cases it was scored on.
questions.correct_explanation: Scoring a tool on the cases used to tune it is like grading an exam the student has already seen: the 98% shows how well it fits those 200, not how many new duplicates it will catch. Validation needs known cases held back from tuning. Unmeasured false alarms waste follow-up effort, but the inflated catch rate is what would mislead the audit about misses.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because small tuning sets can limit a tool. But the bigger flaw is scoring it on those same cases, which inflates the result whatever the set's size.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because false alarms matter. But they cost follow-up time; the overstated catch rate hides how many real duplicates the tool would miss.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because vendors publish figures. But a vendor figure from other data would not validate the tool here either.

tips: Eliminate: C looks to a vendor figure that cannot validate the tool on this data, and A blames the set's size rather than how it was scored.
Final two: D beats B because a catch rate measured on tuning cases overstates performance; false alarms waste time, while hidden misses mislead the audit.
Exam cue: validate an audit AI tool on known cases it never saw while being tuned, just as models are tested on held-out data.

questions.subtopic: 3D Data quality and analytics. Setting an audit tool's threshold
questions.question: Validating its anomaly tool on known cases, a Guyanese gold exporter's audit team finds a higher threshold cuts false alarms by 80% but raises missed fraud from 5% to 30%. Which threshold choice is BEST?

options.A: Adopt the higher threshold, since follow-up effort falls by 80%
options.B: Set the threshold from the engagement's tolerable miss rate
options.C: Keep the vendor's default threshold to avoid any tuning bias
options.D: Adopt the higher threshold and disclose the 30% miss rate

questions.key_concept: An audit AI tool's threshold trades false alarms against misses; the team sets it from the miss rate the engagement objective can tolerate.
questions.pre_read: Weigh what each error costs this engagement before choosing.
questions.correct_explanation: A threshold trades false alarms against misses, so the choice follows what the engagement must not miss. For fraud testing at a gold exporter, a tool missing 30% of known fraud may not support the planned conclusion, so the team sets the threshold from the miss rate the objective can tolerate and plans other tests for the rest. Disclosing a 30% miss rate is honest, but it does not make an unsupportable conclusion supportable.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because false alarms consume effort. But effort saved is not the objective; missing almost a third of known fraud undermines reliance.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it avoids the team's own choices. But the vendor's default was not set for this data or this engagement's risk.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it is transparent. But disclosure explains a weakness; it does not give enough evidence for a fraud conclusion.

tips: Eliminate: A sets the threshold by effort rather than by the objective, and C defers to a default chosen for other data.
Final two: B beats D because the threshold must fit what the engagement can afford to miss; disclosing a high miss rate does not make reliance supportable.
Exam cue: an audit AI tool's threshold is an audit judgment. Measure both error types, then set it by the misses the objective can tolerate.

questions.subtopic: 3D Data quality and analytics. Tuning on work papers
questions.question: A North Macedonian state railway's audit function plans to fine-tune its approved language model on five years of work papers, including staff disciplinary records, to draft findings in house style. What is the GREATEST concern?

options.A: The tuned model may repeat personal details in other auditors' drafts
options.B: The tuned model will need validation before its drafts are relied on
options.C: Five years of work papers may carry an outdated house style
options.D: Fine-tuning may cost more than writing a house style guide

questions.key_concept: Fine-tuning on work papers can make a model memorize and later reproduce confidential personal data, a confidentiality risk beyond output quality.
questions.pre_read: Ask where the training data goes once a model has been tuned on it.
questions.correct_explanation: Fine-tuned models can memorize parts of their training text and reproduce it when prompted, so disciplinary records in the work papers could surface in drafts for other engagements and users without a need to know. That is a confidentiality harm to named staff that no later review can undo. Validating the tuned model before reliance is needed too, but review catches a quality gap; it cannot recall a disclosure.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because any audit AI tool is validated before reliance. But validation checks draft quality; it does not stop memorized personal data from leaking.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because style changes. But an outdated style is a quality nuisance, fixable in review, not a harm to people.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because cost matters. But cost is a business choice; exposing disciplinary records harms staff and the audit function's credibility.

tips: Eliminate: C is a style problem that review fixes, and D is a cost choice rather than a risk to people.
Final two: A beats B because memorized personal data can leak into later drafts; validation tests draft quality but cannot recall a disclosure.
Exam cue: training or tuning on audit data puts that data inside the model. Ask what personal or confidential content could resurface, and to whom.

questions.subtopic: 3D Data quality and analytics. An AI service's web-search feature
questions.question: A Greenlandic municipality's audit team finds its approved AI service's web-search feature sends prompt text to a search provider outside the contract. What should the chief audit executive do FIRST?

options.A: Allow its use, since the main service is approved under contract
options.B: Strip names from any prompt that might trigger a web search
options.C: Ask the vendor to confirm the search provider deletes queries
options.D: Disable web search for audit work until its data path is assessed

questions.key_concept: An AI service's approval covers data paths its contract covers; features that send audit data to outside providers need assessment first.
questions.pre_read: Trace where the audit data goes when the feature runs.
questions.correct_explanation: The approval covered the AI service under its contract terms; the search feature sends audit data to a provider those terms do not cover, so the approval does not extend to it. Disabling the feature for audit work keeps data inside the approved boundary while the path is assessed. Stripping names leaves context that can still identify people and does nothing for confidential findings.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the service is approved. But approval rested on contract terms that do not reach the outside search provider.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it reduces personal data. But context can still identify people, and confidential audit facts leave anyway.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it seeks assurance. But a vendor's word about a provider outside the contract is not an enforceable term.

tips: Eliminate: A extends an approval past the contract it rested on, and C relies on a vendor's word with no contract behind it.
Final two: D beats B because the feature sends audit data outside the approved boundary; stripping names still lets confidential findings and context leave.
Exam cue: an approved AI service is approved under its terms. A feature that sends data elsewhere is outside the approval until assessed.

questions.subtopic: 3E Outputs and reports. Effect of a precision drop
questions.question: An IS auditor finds that the precision of a Papua New Guinean electoral commission's model, which flags voter-roll entries as duplicates for removal, fell from 0.88 to 0.61. Which statement BEST describes the finding's effect?

options.A: The model now misses more of the duplicate entries it should flag
options.B: Nearly four in ten flagged entries may be genuine voters struck off
options.C: Voter-roll data may have drifted from the model's training data
options.D: No alert limit was set for a fall in the model's precision

questions.key_concept: A finding's effect translates the AI metric into consequences: falling precision means more false flags acted on, not more missed cases.
questions.pre_read: Define the metric in plain words before choosing what it means for people.
questions.correct_explanation: Precision is the share of flagged entries that really are duplicates, so a fall to 0.61 means about 39% of flags now point at genuine, separate voters who could be wrongly removed from the roll. That is the effect in human terms. Saying the model misses more duplicates describes recall, which a precision figure does not measure.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because missed duplicates sound like the risk. But that is recall; a precision figure shows wrong flags, not how many duplicates went unflagged.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because drift often lowers precision. But drift is a mechanism, not the effect, and nothing in the finding establishes it.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it names a control gap. But a missing alert limit is the cause; the effect is what the decline does to voters.

tips: Eliminate: C explains how the decline might happen, and D names the control gap, which is the cause.
Final two: B beats A because precision measures how many flags are right; how many duplicates were missed is recall, which this figure cannot show.
Exam cue: translate an AI metric before writing its effect. Precision counts actions taken on false flags; recall counts real cases missed.

questions.subtopic: 3E Outputs and reports. Cause of an agent's overweight bookings
questions.question: A Vanuatu freight airline's AI booking agent accepted 40 shipments above the 70 kg parcel limit in its instructions; the cargo system enforces no weight cap. Which cause should the IS auditor report as PRIMARY?

options.A: The agent's model misread or ignored the weight limit in its instructions
options.B: Staff did not check the cargo system's bookings against the cap
options.C: The limit relied on instructions, with no cap in the cargo system
options.D: A vendor model update changed how the agent follows its instructions

questions.key_concept: When an AI agent breaks a limit held only in its prompt, the reportable cause is the missing system-enforced control, not the model's disobedience.
questions.pre_read: Find where the limit was enforced, if anywhere.
questions.correct_explanation: An instruction in an agent's prompt is guidance the model may misread, ignore or be manipulated into breaking, so it is not a control. The control gap is that nothing outside the model enforced the 70 kg cap in the cargo system. That the model disobeyed is the mechanism; even a model that usually obeys would leave bookings unprotected against misreading or manipulation.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the model broke its instruction. But that is how the failure happened; the cause is relying on an instruction no system enforced.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because review would catch overweight bookings. But review detects after acceptance; the gap that let the shipments through is the missing enforced cap.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because vendor updates can change behavior. But nothing in the facts points to an update; the stated gap is the unenforced limit.

tips: Eliminate: D blames an update the facts never mention, and B names a later check rather than the gap that let the shipments through.
Final two: C beats A because a prompt instruction is not a control; the model disobeying is the mechanism, the unenforced cap is the cause.
Exam cue: when an AI agent exceeds a limit, look for where the limit lived. A limit held only in the prompt is the control gap to report.

questions.subtopic: 3E Outputs and reports. An overdue AI action
questions.question: An Uzbek pension fund's 99%-accurate model suspends pensions of members flagged as deceased; its agreed human-review step is nine months overdue, and the model now covers every region. What should the IS auditor do FIRST?

options.A: Agree a revised date for the overdue step, given the 99% accuracy
options.B: Direct the model owner to pause suspensions until review starts
options.C: Design the human-review step for the model owner to put in place
options.D: Report the late action and its wider exposure to the audit committee

questions.key_concept: Overdue actions on high-impact AI findings go to the audit committee with their exposure; high accuracy does not offset harm at scale.
questions.pre_read: Notice what the overdue step protects, how far the model now reaches and what 99% leaves out.
questions.correct_explanation: A high-impact AI control is nine months late while the model's reach has grown to every region. A 99% accuracy figure does not offset that: at national scale, a small error rate still suspends many living members' pensions with no person checking. Overdue actions of this impact go to the audit committee with the wider exposure; the auditor reports, senior management decides the response and the committee oversees it.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because 99% accuracy sounds safe. But at national scale a small error rate still wrongly suspends many living members; a quietly reset date hides that from the audit committee.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because wrong suspensions harm members. But pausing the model is management's decision; the auditor reports the exposure so management and the committee can act.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it would speed the fix. But designing the control makes the auditor part of management, impairing objectivity.

tips: Eliminate: B has the auditor directing management to stop the model, and C has the auditor designing management's control.
Final two: D beats A because a small error rate across every region still harms many members while the action slips; leaders must see that, not a quietly reset date.
Exam cue: when an AI fix is overdue and the model's reach grows, report both to the audit committee. High accuracy does not offset harm at scale.

questions.subtopic: 3E Outputs and reports. A fix that removes a field
questions.question: An Angolan mobile-money lender's loan model declined rural applicants far more often; management removed the home-province field and asks to close the finding. What is the IS auditor's GREATEST concern?

options.A: Applicants may be scored less accurately without the field
options.B: Other inputs may still reveal where applicants live
options.C: The removal may have gone live without change approval
options.D: Management, not the IS auditor, chose how to fix the model

questions.key_concept: Removing a sensitive field does not remove bias carried by proxies; a fairness finding closes on group outcomes, not on the feature list.
questions.pre_read: Read the finding as an outcome, then ask whether the action taken is sure to change that outcome.
questions.correct_explanation: Removing a field does not remove what it carried: phone type, top-up locations or language can still stand in for where applicants live, so rural applicants may still be declined far more often. The finding closes only when rural and urban decline rates since the change show the gap has gone. Less accurate scoring is a trade-off for the owner to weigh, not evidence the unfair outcome ended.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because removing an input can cost accuracy. But that is the owner's trade-off; the finding concerns rural declines, which proxies may keep high.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because model changes need approval. But nothing suggests the change bypassed control; the open question is whether the bias is gone.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it sounds like a gap. But choosing the fix is management's role; the IS auditor verifies whether it worked.

tips: Eliminate: C assumes a change-control gap nothing points to, and D objects to management choosing its own fix, which is its role.
Final two: B beats A because other inputs can carry what the removed field did, so the rural gap may persist; lower accuracy is the owner's trade-off.
Exam cue: removing a sensitive field is not a fairness fix by itself. Expect proxies, and close bias findings on group outcomes since the change.

questions.subtopic: 3E Outputs and reports. Tool rating versus observation
questions.question: Three days' observation shows Isle of Man bank staff bulk-clearing a payment model's flags unread; the audit's AI tool, reading only flag statuses, rates the review effective. Which conclusion is BEST for the IS auditor?

options.A: The control is ineffective, with a note on why the tool disagrees
options.B: Accept the tool's rating, since it analyzed the whole year's population
options.C: Report both ratings and let management decide which one applies
options.D: Rerun the tool with revised prompts until its rating matches

questions.key_concept: An audit AI tool's rating is an input; when direct evidence contradicts it, the auditor concludes on the evidence and documents why.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the tool could see in its data and what only observation could see.
questions.correct_explanation: The tool read only flag statuses, and a flag cleared unread has the same status as one reviewed with care. Observation shows the review does not operate as intended, and the auditor owns the conclusion. Noting why the tool's rating differs keeps the work papers defensible. Full-population coverage cannot outweigh evidence the data never captured.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because full-population analytics sound stronger than three days of observation. But the tool saw only statuses; a flag cleared unread looks the same as one reviewed with care.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it seems balanced. But the conclusion is the auditor's to reach; management does not choose the audit's ratings.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because a better prompt may help. But tuning a tool until it agrees is not evidence; observation already shows the failure.

tips: Eliminate: C hands the audit's conclusion to management, and D adjusts the tool until it gives the wanted answer.
Final two: A beats B because the tool judged only flag statuses; an unread clearance has the same status as a careful one, so the auditor's evidence decides.
Exam cue: an audit AI tool's rating is input, never the conclusion. When direct evidence contradicts it, conclude on the evidence and record why they differ.

questions.subtopic: 3E Outputs and reports. AI-drafted recommendation
questions.question: Reviewing AI-drafted report text on a Gabonese timber firm's injury-risk model, an IS audit manager sees a recommendation telling the model owner to retrain with a named oversampling method. What is the manager's BEST response?

options.A: Keep the method, since it is a sound fix for the model
options.B: Keep the method, and disclose that an AI tool drafted it
options.C: Reword it as an outcome, leaving the method to the owner
options.D: Ask the owner to trial the method before the report is issued

questions.key_concept: Audit recommendations on AI state the outcome to achieve; the model owner chooses the fix, even when an AI tool drafted a method.
questions.pre_read: Ask who would own the fix if the report prescribes the method.
questions.correct_explanation: Whoever drafted it, the recommendation is the auditor's, and prescribing a retraining method designs the model fix, which belongs to the model owner and could impair the auditor's objectivity in later audits. The manager has it reworded as the outcome to achieve, such as a cap on missed high-risk cases, leaving the method to the owner. Disclosing the AI drafting tells readers how the text was made; it does not make a design recommendation acceptable.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the method may well work. But choosing how to retrain is the owner's decision; prescribing it puts the auditor in the design role.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because AI use should be disclosed. But disclosure explains how the text was made; it does not fix a recommendation that designs the model.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because testing first seems careful. But it still makes the owner trial the auditor's design instead of choosing their own fix.

tips: Eliminate: A keeps an auditor-designed fix because it seems sound, and D still pushes the auditor's chosen method onto the owner.
Final two: C beats B because disclosing that AI drafted the text changes nothing in it; the recommendation would still design the owner's fix.
Exam cue: AI-drafted report text gets the same review as any draft. Recommendations say what must be achieved; the model owner chooses how.

questions.subtopic: 3A Audit planning and design. A staff assistant opened to customers
questions.question: An Icelandic district-heating utility's generative AI staff assistant, rated low risk in the audit universe, will start answering customers' billing questions with no model change. What should MOST drive the IS audit manager's new rating?

options.A: The novelty of generative AI for the utility's customers
options.B: The assistant's measured accuracy on staff billing questions so far
options.C: Its unchanged model and data since the low staff-use rating
options.D: How likely wrong answers are to harm customers who act on them

questions.key_concept: AI audit universe ratings follow each use; a model reused for a new audience is re-rated by the likelihood and impact of harm to them.
questions.pre_read: Notice what changes in this plan and what stays the same.
questions.correct_explanation: AI risk belongs to a use, not only to a model. The same assistant will now answer customers, who cannot spot a wrong bill explanation the way staff can and may pay or dispute on the strength of it, so the rating follows how likely and how harmful its errors are for them. Accuracy measured on staff questions comes from a different audience asking different questions, so it cannot set the new rating.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because customers are new to such tools. But novelty is not risk; ratings follow the likelihood and impact of harm.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it is measured evidence. But it comes from staff, who can spot errors; customers ask differently and act on the answers.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because nothing technical changed. But risk attaches to the use: a new audience changes who is harmed and how.

tips: Eliminate: A ranks by novelty, which is not risk, and C carries over a rating set for a different audience.
Final two: D beats B because accuracy on staff questions says little about harm to customers, who ask differently and act on the answers.
Exam cue: a new audience is a new AI use. Re-rate it by how likely and how harmful its errors are for the people now relying on it.

questions.subtopic: 3A Audit planning and design. Scores outliving a retired model
questions.question: A Croatian motorway operator retired its bridge-corrosion model in March, yet its last scores still set each bridge's inspection interval. How should the IS audit manager BEST treat it in the AI audit universe?

options.A: Remove it, since a retired model no longer runs or retrains
options.B: Keep it, rated low risk because its stored scores no longer change
options.C: Keep it, ranked by the decisions its stored scores drive today
options.D: Move it to next year, once the decommissioning review is complete

questions.key_concept: AI stays in the audit universe while its outputs drive decisions; stored predictions go stale as conditions change, even after the model is retired.
questions.pre_read: Read what retirement changed and what it did not.
questions.correct_explanation: A model's risk lasts as long as its outputs drive decisions. Retiring the code did not retire the scores: they still set how often each bridge is inspected, and as bridges age, those frozen scores grow stale, raising the likelihood of missed corrosion. So the use stays in the universe, ranked by that likelihood and the impact of the decisions it drives. Rating it low because the scores never change gets it backwards.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the model is switched off. But its stored scores still set inspection intervals, so the use and its risk continue.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because nothing in the model can change now. But frozen predictions about aging bridges grow less accurate each month, so their risk rises rather than falls.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because a decommissioning review seems the natural point to judge the model. But the intervals rest on the scores now, so waiting a year leaves a live use unplanned.

tips: Eliminate: A treats retirement as the end of the use, and D defers a use whose outputs drive decisions today.
Final two: C beats B because scores frozen in March grow stale as bridges age; fixed predictions about changing assets raise risk, not lower it.
Exam cue: a retired model whose outputs still drive decisions stays in the audit universe. Rank it by likelihood and impact; frozen outputs grow stale, so likelihood rises.

questions.subtopic: 3A Audit planning and design. A model that retrains weekly
questions.question: An IS auditor's scope for a Mongolian cashmere trader's price-forecast model, retrained weekly on new auction data, covers the current version's code, accuracy and access controls. What is the GREATEST scope weakness?

options.A: Checks on each week's new model before its release go untested
options.B: The code review may need a specialist in time-series forecasting libraries
options.C: Accuracy tests may not cover every region the trader buys in
options.D: Access controls cover the model but not its weekly forecast reports

questions.key_concept: A model that retrains is a new model each time; scope covers the retraining and release process, not only the current version.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the planned tests would cover across the whole period.
questions.correct_explanation: A model retrained every week is a new model every week, so testing the current version's code and accuracy covers one of the many weekly versions that produced forecasts during the audit period. Retraining changes the model without any code change, so the scope must cover how each weekly version is built, validated and released. Testing accuracy region by region refines work on one version; it says nothing about the others.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because forecasting code can be specialized. But that is a staffing question for planning, not a gap in what the audit covers.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because buying regions differ. But it refines a test of one version, while the weekly retrains that produced the others go unexamined.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because reports can reveal prices. But report access is minor beside the many weekly model versions the scope never reaches.

tips: Eliminate: B is a staffing question rather than scope, and D adds a minor access point beside the model's weekly changes.
Final two: A beats C because region coverage refines a test of one version; weekly retraining produced many models the scope never reaches.
Exam cue: a retrain is a change even with no code change. Scope an AI audit across every version that ran, through retraining and release.

questions.subtopic: 3A Audit planning and design. A layered vendor chain
questions.question: A Laotian microfinance firm's loan-help assistant, from a local vendor, runs on a global provider's foundation model, which is retuned several times a year. Which third-party element is MOST important for the IS auditor's scope?

options.A: The foundation model's training data and safety-tuning methods
options.B: The local vendor's service levels and data-handling terms
options.C: How the firm learns of and retests foundation model updates
options.D: The local vendor's security certificate for its hosting

questions.key_concept: For layered AI supply chains, scope how the organization detects and retests upstream foundation model changes, not internals it cannot see.
questions.pre_read: Trace each party in the chain and what each one controls.
questions.correct_explanation: The firm cannot inspect the global provider, but it owns its use of the assistant. A foundation model update reaches the firm through the local vendor and can change answers without any change the firm makes, so the scope must test how the firm learns of each update and retests before relying on it. Service levels and data terms matter, but they do not show whether upstream model changes are caught.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the base model shapes every answer. But the firm cannot see those internals; audit what it controls, including its oversight of changes.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the contract governs the vendor. But service and data terms do not show how upstream model updates are detected and retested.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it is an attestation. But a hosting certificate covers infrastructure, not how the assistant behaves after a model update.

tips: Eliminate: A asks for internals the firm cannot obtain, and D offers a hosting certificate that says nothing about model behavior.
Final two: C beats B because contract terms with the local vendor do not show whether updates to the underlying model are caught and retested.
Exam cue: with layered AI vendors, scope what the organization controls: how it learns of upstream model changes and retests before relying on them.

questions.subtopic: 3A Audit planning and design. A specialist's jailbreak tests
questions.question: IS audit's independent specialist found all 500 jailbreak attempts on a vendor model's API failed; a Tanzanian mobile bank's assistant app adds a system prompt to that model. What should the IS auditor do FIRST?

options.A: Ask the vendor to confirm the API model matches the app's model
options.B: Have the specialist rerun the tests through the bank's own app
options.C: Rely on the result, since the bank's app calls the vendor model
options.D: Rely on the result, since the specialist is independent and qualified

questions.key_concept: Judge a specialist's AI test against the system as deployed; bare model API results do not carry over to the app wrapping it.
questions.pre_read: Read the test conditions as closely as the result.
questions.correct_explanation: Using an expert's work means judging whether the method fits the objective. The bank's app adds its own system prompt, and may add data or tools, each of which can change how the model responds, so an attack the bare model refuses can succeed through the app. Rerunning the tests through the app checks the assistant customers use. Sharing one underlying model does not carry API results over.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the vendor knows its model. But a vendor's confirmation is a claim, and the same model can behave differently inside the app.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the model is the same. But the app adds its own prompt and may add data or tools, which can change how attacks land.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the specialist is vetted and independent. But objectivity and skill do not extend tests to a channel never tried.

tips: Eliminate: A swaps a test for the vendor's assurance, and D weighs who ran the tests instead of what they covered.
Final two: B beats C because the app's own system prompt, and any data or tools it adds, can change how the model responds; API results do not carry over to the deployed assistant.
Exam cue: before relying on an AI specialist's result, check that the tests hit the system as deployed: channel, prompts, data, users and version.

questions.subtopic: 3A Audit planning and design. A specialist's fairness measure
questions.question: The IS auditor's specialist calls a Namibian housing lender's credit model fair because approval rates match across regions; policy requires creditworthy applicants to be refused equally often everywhere. What should the IS auditor do FIRST?

options.A: Accept the conclusion, since matching approval rates meet the policy
options.B: Report the model as fair across regions, naming the measure used
options.C: Ask the model owner which fairness measure the audit should apply
options.D: Have wrongful decline rates by region measured against the policy

questions.key_concept: A specialist's fairness result supports the audit only when it measures what the policy requires; fairness measures can disagree.
questions.pre_read: Check what each fairness figure actually measures.
questions.correct_explanation: Fairness measures answer different questions and can disagree: approval rates can match across regions while creditworthy applicants in one region are wrongly declined far more often, when regions differ in creditworthiness. The policy is about those wrongful declines, so the specialist's work supports a conclusion only once they are measured by region. Asking the model owner to pick the measure would hand audit criteria to the auditee when the policy already sets them.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because matching rates look like equal treatment. But the policy is about wrongful declines, which equal approval rates can hide when regions differ.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it discloses the method. But disclosure does not make approval-rate parity show what the lender's policy requires.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because owners turn fairness into measurable criteria. But the policy already sets the measure, and the IS auditor selects the audit criteria without the auditee's agreement.

tips: Eliminate: A lets approval-rate parity stand in for the policy's test, and B reports a conclusion the measure used cannot support.
Final two: D beats C because the policy already sets the fairness measure; owners set use-level criteria, but the IS auditor selects the audit criteria and needs no auditee agreement.
Exam cue: fairness measures can disagree. Check that a specialist measured what the policy requires before calling a model fair.

questions.subtopic: 3A Audit planning and design. An audit agent's system access
questions.question: An audit team's planned AI agent will query a Qatari cold-chain distributor's ERP system for evidence, using a finance service account that can also post entries. What should the chief audit executive require FIRST?

options.A: Read-only access limited to the data the audit needs
options.B: A log of every action the agent takes, reviewed weekly
options.C: A filter that strips instruction-like text from records the agent reads
options.D: A system prompt forbidding the agent to post entries

questions.key_concept: An audit AI agent gets least-privilege, read-only access enforced by the system, so it cannot change the records the audit examines.
questions.pre_read: Consider how the audit's own tools could affect the auditee's records.
questions.correct_explanation: An agent can do anything its account allows, and instructions planted in the records it reads can steer it past its own instructions; filters for such text miss reworded versions. If the agent posted or changed an entry, the audit would alter the very records it tests and could cause errors in the distributor's books. A read-only account scoped to the audit's data enforces the limit in the system, whatever the agent reads.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it records what happened. But weekly review comes after an entry is posted; it detects changes to auditee data rather than preventing them.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it blocks planted instructions. But filters miss reworded text, and the agent could still post entries through its own error.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it targets posting directly. But a prompt is an instruction, not a control; planted text can override it, and the account still allows posting.

tips: Eliminate: B finds unwanted postings only after they happen, and C screens planted text but leaves the account able to post entries.
Final two: A beats D because a prompt is an instruction the agent can be steered past; read-only access blocks posting whatever the agent reads.
Exam cue: give audit AI agents the narrowest system-enforced access. Filters and prompts can be bypassed, and audit tools must not alter auditee data.

questions.subtopic: 3A Audit planning and design. A downloaded open-weight model
questions.question: A Kyrgyz gold miner's senior IS auditor wants to analyze confidential logs on an audit laptop using an open-weight model downloaded from a public hub. What should the IS audit manager do FIRST?

options.A: Allow it, since the confidential logs stay on the audit laptop
options.B: Have the tool's origin and file integrity assessed
options.C: Require the auditor to save prompts and outputs in the work papers
options.D: Compare its results with an approved cloud tool on the same logs

questions.key_concept: An audit AI tool's supply chain is part of its approval: a downloaded model is assessed for source and integrity before audit use.
questions.pre_read: List the risks this tool brings into the audit environment.
questions.correct_explanation: Keeping data on the laptop addresses one risk, confidentiality, but the use is still unapproved. Model files from public hubs can carry malicious code that runs when loaded, or hidden behaviors from tampered weights, and an unvetted model has not been shown to analyze logs reliably. The manager has the model's origin and integrity assessed before approving its audit use, so no engagement relies on it unchecked. Local processing cannot make an untrusted model safe.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the logs stay on the device. But a tampered model file can run malicious code locally, and nobody has approved the use.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because records support review. But documenting the use of an unvetted, unapproved model does not make it safe or reliable.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because comparison looks like validation. But running the model to compare loads the unchecked file, which is when malicious code would run.

tips: Eliminate: C documents a use nobody approved, and D runs the unchecked file before anyone knows it is safe.
Final two: B beats A because local processing solves confidentiality only; a model from a public hub can carry malicious code or tampered behavior.
Exam cue: approve audit AI tools on more than data location. A downloaded model is outside software: check its origin and integrity first.

questions.subtopic: 3B Testing and sampling. Design of a fairness alert
questions.question: A Costa Rican arts council's fairness control alerts when its grant-screening model's overall rejection rate moves more than 3 percentage points from last year's. What is the IS auditor's BEST conclusion about this control's design?

options.A: Its 3-point limit may be too wide to catch meaningful changes
options.B: It needs operating evidence for the period before design is judged
options.C: It cannot detect a gap between groups if the total stays level
options.D: It is sound, since it compares results with a historical baseline

questions.key_concept: A fairness control must measure outcomes by group; an overall rate can hold steady while one group is harmed.
questions.pre_read: Walk the control through the risk it is meant to catch.
questions.correct_explanation: Fairness risk is about differences between groups, and an overall rejection rate can stay steady while one group's rejections rise and another's fall. Walking the control through that risk shows it cannot see the harm it exists to catch, so the design is deficient whatever its limit. Tightening the limit would still watch only the overall rate, so it would not remove the blind spot.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because limits matter. But any limit on the overall rate still misses group gaps; the flaw is what is measured, not how tightly.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because operation needs testing. But design is judged first; a control that cannot see group gaps fails before operation matters.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because baselines catch change. But last year's overall rate says nothing about how this year's groups compare.

tips: Eliminate: B reverses the order of design and operation testing, and D accepts a baseline that measures the wrong thing.
Final two: C beats A because a tighter limit on the overall rate still cannot see one group's rejections rising while another's fall.
Exam cue: test an AI control's design against the specific risk. Fairness controls must measure by group; totals can hide harm.

questions.subtopic: 3B Testing and sampling. A drift monitor that watches inputs
questions.question: An Ethiopian flower exporter's freight-demand model has its tolerance set on forecast error, but its drift monitor watches only inputs and has not alerted in a year. What should the IS auditor do FIRST?

options.A: Accept the year without alerts as evidence the model stayed accurate
options.B: Confirm the input monitor ran on every day of the year
options.C: Obtain the model owner's statement that forecast error stayed within tolerance
options.D: Recompute recent forecast error and compare it with the tolerance

questions.key_concept: Input-drift monitoring does not measure performance; test the metric the tolerance names, since relationships can change while inputs look stable.
questions.pre_read: Read a monitor's design before trusting its record.
questions.correct_explanation: The tolerance is set on forecast error, but the monitor watches only inputs. Inputs can look stable while the link between them and freight demand changes, for example when airlines change schedules, so error can breach the tolerance with no alert. The auditor first recomputes recent forecast error against the tolerance. Confirming that the input monitor ran daily tests the operation of a check that does not measure what the tolerance protects.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the monitor never alerted. But it watches inputs; error can rise while inputs look stable.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because operation over the period is standard. But a daily check on inputs still cannot show forecast error met the tolerance.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the owner knows the model. But a statement is an assertion; only recomputed forecast error shows the tolerance was met.

tips: Eliminate: A reads silence from an input monitor as proof of accuracy, and C rests on the owner's assertion instead of evidence.
Final two: D beats B because daily operation of an input monitor cannot show forecast error stayed within tolerance; only recomputed error can.
Exam cue: match the monitor to the tolerance. Input drift checks can stay quiet while performance falls, so measure the metric the tolerance names.

questions.subtopic: 3B Testing and sampling. Sampling unit for an agent
questions.question: An IS auditor will sample a Dominican resort group's AI agent, which onboards each new supplier through 10 to 30 tool calls, such as sanctions checks and bank-detail updates. Which sampling unit is BEST?

options.A: Whole supplier onboardings, tracing every tool call within each
options.B: Supplier records the agent itself marked as successfully onboarded
options.C: Individual tool calls drawn at random from the agent's call log
options.D: Onboardings the sanctions check flagged, with their final records

questions.key_concept: For an AI agent, sample whole tasks and trace every step, because errors arise in the order and gaps between tool calls.
questions.pre_read: Decide what a single decision is for this system before choosing what to sample.
questions.correct_explanation: An agent's control risks sit in the sequence: whether the sanctions check ran before bank details changed, or whether a step was skipped. A sample of whole onboardings lets the auditor trace each one end to end and judge it as one decision. Tool calls drawn at random each look normal on their own and cannot show order, omissions or how one step's result shaped the next.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because these are completed cases. But the agent marked them itself, so failures it judged as successes stay hidden.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because calls are what the log records. But single calls lose their context; skipped or out-of-order steps show only in the whole task.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because flagged cases seem riskiest. But onboardings the check cleared, where errors go unnoticed, are left out.

tips: Eliminate: B lets the agent's own success marks define the population, and D keeps only cases the sanctions check flagged.
Final two: A beats C because random calls each look normal alone; only a whole onboarding shows a skipped check or steps in the wrong order.
Exam cue: sample an AI agent by task, not by tool call. Its errors live in sequence, omissions and how one step feeds the next.

questions.subtopic: 3B Testing and sampling. Scoring answers that vary between runs
questions.question: Testing a Georgian wine-export agency's chatbot against current labeling rules, an IS auditor asks each of 40 questions five times; one question gets a wrong answer once. How should the auditor BEST treat that question?

options.A: As a pass, since four of its five answers were correct
options.B: As an exception, since exporters can receive the wrong answer
options.C: As a pass, unless the wrong answer recurs on further asking
options.D: As untested, until the chatbot's vendor explains why answers vary

questions.key_concept: Generative AI answers vary run to run; a wrong answer in any run is an exception, because users can receive it.
questions.pre_read: Decide what one test result means when the same input can give different outputs.
questions.correct_explanation: Because the chatbot generates each reply with some randomness, one question has a range of possible answers, and any exporter may get the wrong one. A wrong answer in one of five runs is an error the chatbot actually gives, so the question is an exception, and the runs help estimate how often it happens. Treating four correct answers as a pass takes the majority as the chatbot's answer, but exporters receive every variant.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because most answers were right. But exporters get whichever answer is generated; a wrong one in five still reaches some of them.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because one wrong answer can look like a fluke. But varying output may not repeat on demand; the wrong answer was still given.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the variation needs explaining. But the auditor already has a test result; the vendor's account does not change what exporters received.

tips: Eliminate: C waits for an error that may not repeat on demand, and D sets aside a result the auditor already has.
Final two: B beats A because exporters receive every variant; four correct answers in five still leave a wrong one reaching some exporters.
Exam cue: when a model's answers vary, every run is a test item. A wrong answer in any run is an exception, not noise outvoted by the majority.

questions.subtopic: 3B Testing and sampling. Rule query or anomaly tool
questions.question: An IS auditor can test all 120,000 credit limits a Serbian lender's model set this year; policy caps each at three times monthly income, and the audit's anomaly tool is validated. Which approach is BEST?

options.A: Test a statistical sample of 60 limits against the policy cap
options.B: Run the validated anomaly tool over the limits and test its flags
options.C: Review the model's validation report for how often it breached the cap
options.D: Run a query comparing every limit with the policy cap

questions.key_concept: When a policy gives an exact rule, a full-population query tests it completely; anomaly detection finds the unusual, not every breach.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the policy lets you test exactly.
questions.correct_explanation: The policy gives an exact rule, so a query can test every limit against it and list each breach. An anomaly tool, however well validated, flags what looks unusual compared with the rest; if the model breaches the cap often, breaches look normal and go unflagged, and its misses stay untested. AI analytics suit patterns no rule can state, not a test a simple rule performs completely.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because sampling is standard. But every limit can be tested against an exact rule, which a sample of 60 cannot match.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the tool is validated and covers every limit. But anomaly tools flag rarity; frequent breaches look normal, and unflagged limits stay untested.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because builders test their models. But pre-release validation does not show this year's production limits met the cap.

tips: Eliminate: A samples where every item can be checked against an exact rule, and C relies on builders' testing before release.
Final two: D beats B because an anomaly tool flags what is rare; if breaches are common they look normal, so a rule query is the complete test.
Exam cue: use simple rules for full-population tests of exact criteria. Keep AI analytics for patterns rules cannot express; unflagged is not tested.

questions.subtopic: 3B Testing and sampling. A fairness measure's narrowed population
questions.question: A Colombian bank's fairness dashboard compares approval rates by sex using only completed applications; its model asks some applicants for extra documents, and many then withdraw. What should the IS auditor do FIRST?

options.A: Rely on the dashboard, since the bank's own systems generate it
options.B: Recompute approval rates by sex from completed applications in the logs
options.C: Recompute approval rates by sex from all applications, withdrawals included
options.D: Ask the model owner why applicants withdraw after document requests

questions.key_concept: When a model's own actions remove people before the decision, fairness is measured on everyone who applied, not only completed cases.
questions.pre_read: Ask who the metric's population leaves out, and why.
questions.correct_explanation: The model does more than approve or decline: its document requests drive withdrawals, so a measure built on completed applications leaves out people the model effectively turned away. If requests fall more on one sex, the dashboard can look fair while the process is not. Recomputing from all applications, withdrawals included, tests the model's whole effect. Reperforming the dashboard's figures only confirms its arithmetic on the same narrowed population.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the figures are system-generated. But the system applies a definition that leaves out applicants the model's requests drove away.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because reperformance is strong evidence. But it repeats the dashboard's definition, so withdrawals the model caused stay outside the measure.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it seeks the cause. But inquiry comes after evidence; first measure whether withdrawals differ by sex.

tips: Eliminate: A trusts a system's figures without checking what they measure, and D asks for explanations before the evidence is in.
Final two: C beats B because reperforming the dashboard repeats its narrowed population; only all applications show whether document requests drove one sex away.
Exam cue: check how a fairness metric's population was formed. If the model's actions remove people early, recompute from everyone who applied.

questions.subtopic: 3C Evidence collection. Diagnosing a retrieval assistant's answer
questions.question: An Estonian e-government assistant, which answers from a benefit-guidance library, told a resident the wrong application deadline. Which evidence BEST shows the IS auditor whether the error came from the guidance or the model?

options.A: The retrieval log of passages supplied to the model for that answer
options.B: The current benefit guidance on deadlines in the assistant's library
options.C: The library's version history for the benefit guidance on deadlines
options.D: The model card describing the assistant's known limits and error rates

questions.key_concept: For a retrieval assistant, the log of passages supplied to the model separates source errors from generation errors.
questions.pre_read: Trace an answer back through each stage that produced it.
questions.correct_explanation: In a retrieval assistant, each answer is generated from the passages fetched for that question. The retrieval log shows exactly what the model was given: if the passages held the right deadline, the model misstated it; if they held a wrong or outdated one, the fault lies in the guidance or the search. The library's version history shows what the guidance said then, but not which passages this answer drew on.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it is the assistant's source. But today's guidance may differ from what the assistant read when it answered.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it shows what the guidance said at the time. But the assistant may have fetched other passages; only the retrieval log shows which.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it describes known weaknesses. But a general description cannot show what caused this answer.

tips: Eliminate: B shows today's guidance, not what the assistant read then, and D describes the system in general, not this answer.
Final two: A beats C because version history shows what the guidance said, not which passages this answer was built from.
Exam cue: to diagnose a retrieval assistant's answer, get the retrieved passages; they separate errors in the sources from errors in generation.

questions.subtopic: 3C Evidence collection. Support for a model card's claim
questions.question: A Paraguayan job-matching platform's model card states that its ranking model, retrained monthly, was tested for bias across age groups. Which evidence BEST supports this statement for the IS auditor?

options.A: The age-group fairness report from the model's first release
options.B: This version's fairness test results by age group
options.C: The datasheet showing the age mix of this version's training data
options.D: The policy requiring age-group bias tests before each release

questions.key_concept: A model card's claims are the builders' description; the underlying test report, by group and version, is the evidence.
questions.pre_read: Rank the evidence by how directly it shows the claim.
questions.correct_explanation: A model card is the builders' own description, so a claim in it needs the record it summarizes: the fairness test report, with results by age group, for the version now ranking candidates, since monthly retraining replaces earlier versions. The datasheet's age mix shows what the model learned from, not how it ranks older and younger job seekers; a balanced dataset can still produce unequal rankings.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because it is a real fairness test by age. But monthly retraining has replaced that model; the claim must hold for the version now ranking candidates.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because balanced data seems to imply fair results. But training composition shows inputs, not how the model ranks each age group.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it requires testing. But a policy shows intent, not that this version was tested or passed.

tips: Eliminate: A tests a version monthly retraining has replaced, and D shows a requirement, not that it was met.
Final two: B beats C because the training data's age mix shows what the model learned from, not how it ranks each age group.
Exam cue: to support a model card's claim, get the record it summarizes. Data composition is not a test result.

questions.subtopic: 3C Evidence collection. Preserving a continuously learning model
questions.question: A Bahraini Islamic bank's fraud model updates its weights continuously from each confirmed case. Which preservation request BEST lets the IS auditor later rerun the model on decisions from the audit period?

options.A: The training code and the dataset that built the model's first version
options.B: A full copy of the updated model as it stands at fieldwork
options.C: The decision log of each transaction's score and outcome
options.D: Regular snapshots of the model, with the update data between them

questions.key_concept: A continuously learning model has no fixed version; reperforming past decisions needs periodic snapshots and the update data between them.
questions.pre_read: Ask how many different models made decisions during the period.
questions.correct_explanation: A model that learns from every confirmed case is a slightly different model after each update, so one copy taken at fieldwork reproduces only today's decisions. Regular snapshots, with the confirmed cases applied between them, let the auditor rebuild the model as it stood when a past decision was made, or come close, and rerun it. Decision logs record what was decided, but cannot show the model then in force would decide that way.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because it shows how the model began. But thousands of updates have shaped it since; the starting point cannot reproduce later states.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it preserves the model before further change. But it captures only today's state; earlier decisions came from states the updates have replaced.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because logs are strong evidence of what happened. But they record results; rerunning needs the model state that produced them.

tips: Eliminate: A preserves only the starting point of a model that has changed since, and C records results without the model that produced them.
Final two: D beats B because a continuously learning model changes with each case; one copy at fieldwork cannot rerun decisions made months earlier.
Exam cue: a model that keeps learning has no single version. Preserve regular snapshots and the update data between them to rerun past decisions.

questions.subtopic: 3C Evidence collection. Model-written review reasons
questions.question: A Lebanese retailer's warranty assessors must give reasons for accepting the model's claim rejections; the screen pre-fills model-written reasons, which most keep. What is the IS auditor's GREATEST concern with these reasons as evidence?

options.A: They may be too short to explain each rejection fully
options.B: The model-written reasons may contain factual errors about the claims
options.C: They may record the model's text, not any human judgment
options.D: They may not be kept for the whole audit period

questions.key_concept: A pre-filled, model-written reason that reviewers keep evidences the model's text, not human review, and invites automation bias.
questions.pre_read: Ask what each record would look like if no real review took place.
questions.correct_explanation: The reasons field is meant to evidence each assessor's review, but when the screen supplies a model-written reason and most assessors keep it, the field records the model's text, not human judgment. Pre-filled answers also anchor reviewers toward agreement, so the records may reflect automation bias rather than review. The auditor needs other evidence, such as review times, overrides or seeded cases. Errors in the reasons matter, but they do not show whether review happened.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because brief reasons explain little. But length is not the problem; who wrote the reason is.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because generated text can be wrong. But the question is whether the field shows review; even accurate text would be the model's, not the assessor's.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because retention limits evidence. But nothing suggests a retention gap; the reasons' authorship is the issue.

tips: Eliminate: A worries about length when authorship is at issue, and D raises a retention gap nothing suggests.
Final two: C beats B because even accurate model text, kept unchanged, shows acceptance, not the assessor's judgment.
Exam cue: evidence of human review must come from the human. Pre-filled AI text that reviewers keep signals automation bias, not oversight.

questions.subtopic: 3C Evidence collection. An AI tool's account of its own ratings
questions.question: An IS auditor's approved AI tool rated 400 of an Armenian mining company's quarterly access reviews adequate and, when asked, gave a confident rationale for each rating. How should the auditor BEST treat the rationales?

options.A: As leads, checking a sample of ratings against review records
options.B: As evidence, since each rationale cites the review's own content
options.C: As documentation of the tool's method, filed with each rating
options.D: As evidence, since each rationale reads as clear and convincing

questions.key_concept: An AI tool's explanation of its own output is generated text, not a record of its method; verify the output against source records.
questions.pre_read: Separate records of work done from descriptions of it.
questions.correct_explanation: A rationale written on request is new generated text, not a record of how the tool reached its rating; it can sound convincing and still be wrong, or describe reasoning the tool never used. So the ratings and their rationales stay leads until the auditor checks a sample against the access review records. Filing the rationales as the tool's method would document a story about the work, not the work itself.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because quotes look grounded. But citing a review does not show the rating is right; quotes can be wrong or invented.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because method should be documented. But a generated explanation is not a trace of how a rating was made; method comes from version, prompt and inputs.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the reasoning reads well. But fluent, confident text is what such tools produce whether right or wrong; only source records show accuracy.

tips: Eliminate: B takes quotation as proof, and D takes persuasiveness as proof; neither shows a rating is right.
Final two: A beats C because a rationale generated on request is not a trace of the tool's method; the ratings still need checking against records.
Exam cue: an AI's explanation of itself is more output, not evidence. Corroborate the result with source records.

questions.subtopic: 3C Evidence collection. A finding resting on an AI code explanation
questions.question: A draft finding against an Indonesian nickel smelter rests on one line of a production access script that an approved AI tool says grants all users admin rights. What should the IS auditor do FIRST?

options.A: Ask a second approved AI tool to explain the line and compare
options.B: Check the permissions the script has set in the live system
options.C: Ask the smelter's script author to confirm the tool's explanation
options.D: Rely on the explanation, since the tool is approved for audit work

questions.key_concept: An AI tool's explanation of code is a lead; a finding that rests on it needs the effect confirmed in the system.
questions.pre_read: Ask how much of the finding depends on this one piece of evidence.
questions.correct_explanation: A finding resting on one line stands or falls on what that line does, and AI explanations of code can be fluent and wrong, for example by misreading a condition or an exception. Checking the permissions the script actually set in the live system gives evidence of its effect. Approval lets auditors use the tool; it does not verify each output, least of all one a finding depends on.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because a second tool looks independent. But two models can share a misreading, and neither shows what the script actually set.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the author knows the script. But the auditee has an interest in the reading; the system's actual settings are independent evidence.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the tool passed approval. But approval permits use; it does not make each output reliable, especially one a finding rests on.

tips: Eliminate: A swaps one model's reading for another's, and C asks the party with an interest in the reading to confirm it.
Final two: B beats D because approval lets the team use the tool; it does not verify an explanation a finding depends on.
Exam cue: when a conclusion rests on AI-processed evidence, confirm that evidence independently. Tool approval is not verification of each output.

questions.subtopic: 3D Data quality and analytics. A synthetic copy of a decision log
questions.question: Testing which batches a Greek olive-oil exporter's supplier-risk model sent for lab tests, an IS auditor is offered a synthetic log matching the real log's statistics, to protect growers' data. What is the GREATEST concern?

options.A: Rare, high-risk batches may be smoothed out of the copy
options.B: Growers might still be re-identified from the synthetic records
options.C: The data team, not the auditor, generated the synthetic log
options.D: Its records show no selection that actually took place

questions.key_concept: Testing AI decisions needs records of what happened; synthetic data built to match statistics shows no real decision, however faithful.
questions.pre_read: Ask how each record in the offered log came to be.
questions.correct_explanation: A synthetic log is generated to resemble the real one, so none of its records is a choice the supplier-risk model actually made. Tests on it can show patterns, but not whether any real batch was scored, sent for testing or passed over. The auditor needs the real log, with protections such as masked grower names. Losing rare batches is a real weakness, but even a perfect copy would hold no real choices.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because synthetic data often loses rare cases. But even a copy that kept every rare pattern would describe invented batches, not real choices.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because synthetic records can leak personal data. But that is a privacy risk for the exporter; for the audit, no record shows a real choice.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because auditee-prepared data needs checking. But a synthetic log the auditor generated would still show no choice the model made.

tips: Eliminate: B is the exporter's privacy risk, not a flaw in the evidence, and C asks who made the copy, which cannot make it real.
Final two: D beats A because even a synthetic log that kept every rare batch would describe invented cases, not choices the model made.
Exam cue: synthetic data can help test a tool but cannot show what an AI system did. Tests of AI decisions need the real records, protected if needed.

questions.subtopic: 3D Data quality and analytics. A model-inferred attribute in test data
questions.question: For a fairness test of a Spanish gym chain's membership-pricing model, the data team supplies members' sex inferred from names by another model. What is the IS auditor's GREATEST concern in relying on this data?

options.A: The pricing model may use members' names as an input
options.B: Inferring members' sex may breach the gym chain's data-minimization rules
options.C: Inference errors may differ by name origin and distort the comparison
options.D: The name model's vendor terms may not allow this use

questions.key_concept: Attributes inferred by a model are outputs with group-varying errors; validate them before relying on them in audit tests.
questions.pre_read: Ask where each field in the audit data came from and how it was produced.
questions.correct_explanation: The group label driving the test is itself a model's guess. Name-based inference errs more for some names, such as unisex names or names from less common origins, so members can be counted in the wrong group unevenly, masking or inventing a gap. The auditor needs the inference's error rate by group, or a verified sample, before relying on the comparison. Privacy rules matter, but they do not decide whether the result is right.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because names can act as proxies. But that concerns the pricing model's inputs; the question is whether the test data's sex labels are reliable.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because inferring sex touches personal data. But even a permitted use would rest on guessed labels; reliance turns on whether they are right.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because license terms matter. But nothing suggests a breach, and terms do not affect whether the labels are accurate.

tips: Eliminate: A shifts to the pricing model's inputs, and D raises license terms with nothing suggesting a breach.
Final two: C beats B because even a permitted use would rest on guessed labels; uneven inference errors can hide or invent the gap being tested.
Exam cue: when a model inferred the group labels in fairness test data, check its error rate by group first; uneven label errors can hide or invent the gap.

questions.subtopic: 3D Data quality and analytics. A prompt reworded after validation
questions.question: A Zambian copper miner's audit team validated its generative AI invoice-matching tool on 5,000 past invoices, then reworded its prompt to cut false alarms on live invoices. What BEST supports relying on it now?

options.A: A rerun of the validation cases with the reworded prompt
options.B: The vendor's published rate for catching invoice mismatches
options.C: The drop in false alarms since the prompt was reworded
options.D: The original validation, since the tool's model is unchanged

questions.key_concept: A generative audit tool's prompt is part of the tool; rewording it after validation means rerunning the known cases before reliance continues.
questions.pre_read: Note what changed after validation and what each option could actually show.
questions.correct_explanation: A generative tool's prompt is part of the tool: rewording it changes what the model is asked to do, so the validation covered a tool that no longer runs. The rewording came from live invoices, not the validation cases, so rerunning those cases with the new prompt is still a fair test of whether it catches the known mismatches. Relying on the original validation because the model is unchanged ignores the prompt.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it measures mismatches directly. But it comes from the vendor's own data and prompts, not this tool as reworded on the miner's invoices.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because cutting false alarms was the goal. But fewer flags can mean more missed mismatches; false alarms alone cannot show detection held.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the model itself did not change. But the prompt shapes every answer, so a reworded prompt makes the validated tool a different one.

tips: Eliminate: B is the vendor's figure from its own data, and C counts fewer false alarms, which cannot show what the tool now misses.
Final two: A beats D because a generative tool's prompt is part of the tool; with the model unchanged but the prompt reworded, the validated tool no longer runs.
Exam cue: for a generative audit tool, a prompt change is a tool change. Revalidate on known cases before relying on it again.

questions.subtopic: 3D Data quality and analytics. Known cases the tool chose
questions.question: A Tunisian date exporter's audit team validated its AI split-purchase tool on 300 known split purchases, all found earlier by a prior version of the tool. What is the GREATEST concern with this validation?

options.A: The known splits may span too few years to reflect current buying
options.B: The tool's false-alarm rate may make follow-up work costly
options.C: The prior version's results may differ from the current version's
options.D: The known cases hold only splits of kinds the tool can find

questions.key_concept: Known cases chosen by the tool itself cannot reveal its misses; validation sets need cases found independently of the tool.
questions.pre_read: Check how the validation cases were assembled before reading the score.
questions.correct_explanation: A validation set is only as good as the way its cases were found. Every known split here was found by the same tool, so splits its approach misses, such as orders spread across two buyers or several weeks, cannot be in the set, and the measured detection rate will look high whatever the tool misses. False alarms matter for effort, but they do not make the tool's misses visible.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because buying patterns change. But nothing suggests the period is short; the problem is which splits the set can contain at all.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because false alarms waste effort. But they cost time, while a set the tool selected hides the misses that matter for reliance.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because versions differ. But the current version was the one tested; the issue is how the cases were chosen.

tips: Eliminate: A doubts the set's time span with nothing suggesting it is short, and C questions a version difference when the current version was the one tested.
Final two: D beats B because false alarms only cost effort; cases the tool chose for itself hide exactly the misses that reliance depends on.
Exam cue: validate an audit AI tool on cases found independently of it. A test set the tool selected measures only what it already finds.

questions.subtopic: 3D Data quality and analytics. Sharing a loaded assistant
questions.question: A Swiss audit firm's IS auditor built a custom assistant on the firm's approved AI service, loaded it with one client's control documents and shared it firm-wide. What is the GREATEST concern?

options.A: The service vendor may use the client's documents to train its models
options.B: Staff on other engagements can query the client's documents through it
options.C: Its answers may differ when colleagues ask the same question
options.D: Its version and settings may go unrecorded in the work papers

questions.key_concept: Files loaded into a shared AI assistant are retrievable by all its users; access to audit data follows the engagement, not the tool.
questions.pre_read: List every party who can reach the audit data after each step.
questions.correct_explanation: Files loaded into a custom assistant become part of what it can retrieve and quote, so sharing the assistant shares the documents with everyone who can use it, including teams serving other clients. That breaches client confidentiality inside the firm, whatever the vendor's terms. The service is approved, so its terms on training and retention were already assessed; the new exposure is the firm-wide sharing of one client's files.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because vendors may reuse inputs. But the service is approved, so its training terms were assessed; the new exposure is inside the firm.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because generated answers vary. But variation affects reproducibility, not who can read the client's documents.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because records support review. But a documentation gap is minor beside confidential files open to the whole firm.

tips: Eliminate: C is a reproducibility point and D a record-keeping one; neither touches who can read the client's files.
Final two: B beats A because the approved service's vendor terms were already assessed; sharing the assistant opens one client's files to every team.
Exam cue: anything loaded into an AI assistant can be retrieved by whoever can use it. Limit audit assistants to the engagement team.

questions.subtopic: 3D Data quality and analytics. Embeddings of work papers
questions.question: A Maltese pension fund's audit team plans to keep embeddings of confidential work papers in an unapproved vendor's vector database, reasoning they are only numbers. What is the chief audit executive's BEST decision?

options.A: Allow it, since embeddings cannot be turned back into readable text
options.B: Remove names from the papers before embedding them
options.C: Apply the work papers' data rules to the embeddings as well
options.D: Require the vendor to encrypt the vector database at rest

questions.key_concept: Embeddings derived from confidential audit data carry its confidentiality; they stay in approved services under the same rules.
questions.pre_read: Check whether a transformed copy still reveals its source.
questions.correct_explanation: Embeddings are derived from the text and keep much of its meaning: published research has reconstructed much of the original wording from them, and similarity searches reveal what the papers discuss. So they carry the work papers' confidentiality and stay inside approved services under the same data rules. Encryption at rest protects stored disks, but the unapproved vendor still holds and processes the data under terms nobody assessed.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because vectors look meaningless. But inversion attacks can reconstruct much of the original text from embeddings.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because names are the obvious identifiers. But findings and context still identify people and issues, and inversion can recover them.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because encryption is a standard control. But it guards stored disks; the unapproved vendor still processes the data under unassessed terms.

tips: Eliminate: A assumes embeddings cannot be reversed, and B assumes names are all that identifies people.
Final two: C beats D because encryption at rest protects stored disks; the unapproved vendor still holds and processes data derived from confidential papers.
Exam cue: derived AI data, such as embeddings, inherits the source's confidentiality. Keep it inside approved services under the same rules.
